prompt: Write a cranky blog post about trying a bunch of new web calendar apps and finding that none of them do what you need. Include a theory about why so many of them exist.
response:
# I Tried Six Web Calendars So You Don't Have To

I want to be clear about what I need, because I suspect it's the thing making me look unreasonable. I need to put a block of time on a page and have it mean "do not book me here." I need to see the next two weeks in a grid. I need to be able to say "yes" or "no" when someone emails me a time. I need it to be boring, the way a wall calendar is boring, the way a paper appointment book is boring. I need to look at it for four seconds and put it away.

I tried the one with the purple interface first because a friend said "oh, it's so clean." It is clean. It is clean the way a hospital waiting room is clean. You can see every surface. You can see the seams. You can see where they're going to start charging you for the feature you were just using for free, which is "recurring events," which is not a premium feature, that is the *point*. I set up a four-hour block on Tuesday. It rendered as a pale lavender rectangle. I invited a contractor. She told me the link "didn't load right" and she just picked a time. I checked. She picked my Tuesday block. The block was there. The block was visible. The block was *lavender*. I don't know what else to do with a block.

The second one, the one that calls its pricing tiers "plans" with the same energy a CrossFit gym uses the word "journey," actually works. I will give it that. The drag-and-drop is smooth. The week view is legible. But it wants to be my project manager. There's a "task" field on every event. There's a "priority" field. There's a little column on the left called "Focus" where it suggests, with a soft encouraging tone, that I might want to "batch similar activities." I do not have similar activities. I have one activity and it's called "being available." I spent forty-five minutes in the settings looking for the option to turn off the suggestions. The option does not exist. The suggestions are not a feature. They are the product. The calendar is the demo.

The third one I found because it came up in a "best free calendars 2025" listicle, which is its own genre of content marketing where every calendar is "free" in the way that a "free trial" is free, which is to say it is a sample of the thing you're about to buy, and the sample is specifically the part that will make you want to buy the thing. This one let me make events. It let me see events. It did not, I discovered on day four, let me *move* an event to a different day. I could delete it. I could recreate it. I could drag it to a different *time* on the same day. But if the Tuesday thing becomes a Thursday thing, I am making a new thing. I am a new thing. I am starting over.

The fourth one is the one where the mobile app is a different product from the web app, which is the most honest and most infuriating thing about the whole category. You build your life on the desktop. You get a notification. You open the phone. The layout is different. The colors are different. The thing you're trying to tap is in a different place and is a different size and the button that says "confirm" is the button that says "edit." You confirm the edit. Now the event has a new title. Now the event has a location that is just the word "here."

I will address the obvious objection, which is that I am the problem, that I should pick one and learn it, that the learning curve is a one-time cost I'm refusing to pay. I paid it. I gave the purple one a full week. I gave the gym one a full week. The learning curve isn't a one-time cost. It's a recurring tax, because the interface is built around workflows I don't have, and every time I open the app I'm re-learning which icon is "new event" and which icon is "new *project*," and which of the three views is the one where I can actually see Thursday. A paper appointment book has one workflow. I have used it for thirty years. I do not re-learn it.

The fifth one I'll skip because it's the one where you have to be "invited" to a shared calendar, which means I have to email someone a link, they have to accept it, and then for the next six weeks every time I look at my calendar I'm also looking at their events, which I did not consent to, which is not what a calendar is, which is a private surface I'm showing you a window into, not a shared whiteboard.

The sixth one works. I don't know why I'm telling you this. It works, and it's not free, and the free version has a watermark on the .ics export that says "Made with [Product]," which means if I send someone my availability, they see a little brand logo in the metadata, which is fine, which is a reasonable business model, which I will pay for. But it's the sixth one. I have been doing this for three weeks. I have been *installing calendars* for three weeks. I should have just bought the first one that wasn't a demo.

And that's the thing, the theory I keep coming back to: the calendar is technically solved. It's a grid. It's a grid with colored rectangles and a time axis. You can build one in a weekend, and people do, because the developer experience is genuinely good and the problem is small and satisfying. The hard part was never the calendar. The hard part is making it the thing you check every ninety seconds, the thing that lives in your browser tab next to the one with your email, the thing that means you're *in* the ecosystem. The calendar is the front door. The Gantt chart for your life, the focus suggestions, the task fields, the "plans" with the journey language—those are the rooms behind the door. The calendar is the loss leader. You don't buy a calendar. You buy the thing that will eventually send you a notification at 2:00 p.m. saying you have a "focus block" coming up, and you'll open it, and you'll be in the product, and the product will be fine, and the product will cost eleven dollars a month, and the calendar will be the part you can't leave because it's where the Tuesday block lives.

I paid eleven dollars for the sixth one. The Tuesday block is there. It's a solid gray rectangle. It's boring. I can see Thursday from across the room. I put the tab in a folder I don't open.

It's a wall calendar. It has a marker. It's fine.
reasoning:
The user wants a cranky blog post about trying web calendar apps and none of them working. Let me think about what would make this feel real and specific rather than generic.

Main idea: The specific frustration isn't that calendars are bad—it's that they all solve slightly different problems and none solve *your* problem, which is actually pretty simple. The crankiness comes from the gap between "I just want to see when I'm free" and the 47 settings panels you have to configure first.

Hardest objection: "Maybe you're the problem. Maybe you should just pick one and learn it." I need to address this. The answer is: I have tried that. I gave three of them a full week. The problem is that the learning curve isn't a one-time cost you amortize—it's a recurring tax because the UI is designed around workflows you don't have.

Concrete cases: Let me think about specific things that are maddening. The "free" tier that's actually a demo. The one where you can't drag an event to a different day without it becoming a recurring event. The one where "all-day" events render as a thin line at the top of the day and you keep clicking it thinking it's a bug. The one where the mobile app is a different product from the web app. The one where you invite someone and they get a .ics file that doesn't work with Outlook. The one where the week view starts on Monday and you live in a world that starts on Sunday and the setting is buried.

Theory about why so many exist: The calendar is a solved problem technically. It's a grid with colored rectangles. So why 200 of them? Because the calendar is the front door to a workflow. Every company that sells "productivity" needs a calendar to be the thing you check every 90 seconds, and if you're checking it, you're in their ecosystem. The calendar is the loss leader. Also: the developer experience is genuinely good. You can build a calendar in a weekend. The hard part isn't the calendar. The hard part is making it the thing you can't leave. So everyone builds the easy part and competes on the retention tricks.

Let me also think about the specific "what I need" that none of them do. I want: I want to block out a 4-hour "no" slot on Tuesday and Thursday, and I want it to be visually obvious to people I invite that those slots are taken, and I want the thing to not make me feel like I'm managing a project. I want it to be boring. I want it to be like a wall calendar with a marker. The web apps want to be like a Gantt chart for your life.

Tone: cranky but not incoherent. Specific. A little self-aware (the "maybe I'm the problem" thing). Not mean-spirited toward specific companies—more exasperated at the category. I'll keep company names vague or generic to avoid it reading as a hit piece, or I'll use them loosely. Actually, for a blog post, naming a couple makes it feel real. Let me use "the one with the purple UI" and "the one that calls its pricing tiers 'plans' like a gym." Keep it light.

Length: This should be a real blog post. Maybe 700-900 words. Enough to go through 4-5 apps with specific complaints, land the "maybe I'm the problem" beat, and develop the theory. Not so long it becomes a listicle.

prompt: Write a personal essay about the meaning of life, framed around a workshop or dinner conversation. I'm tired of tidy answers and want something thoughtful.
response:
# The Load-Bearing Wall

The workshop was a converted barn outside of Millbrook, and the floor was the kind of dirt that got packed hard under the workbenches but turned to mud in the corners. We were doing a weekend course in Japanese joinery—tenon, mortise, the whole vocabulary of wood that holds without nails—and by Saturday afternoon the air smelled of cedar shavings and the particular sweet rot of wet wood chips. I was at the bench trying to cut a wedge tenon for a small shelf, and my chisel had slipped twice, so the wood was a little ragged at the shoulder, and I was annoyed in the small, private way that makes you want to quit the whole thing.

That's when Margot asked the question. Not directly. She was two benches down, fitting a dado joint into a piece of white oak, and she'd set her mallet down and was looking at the joint the way you look at a tooth you're trying to decide whether to pull. "My husband used to say the meaning of life was the meaning of your marriage," she said. "And I believed him for thirty-one years." She said it flatly, the way you'd report the weather. Then she picked the mallet back up and tapped the joint home.

The room didn't go quiet, exactly. People were still cutting, still measuring, still arguing about whether a kanna was a file or a plane. But I felt the question land. It had been hanging over the whole weekend in a way I hadn't noticed. The instructor, a quiet man named Dale who'd taught for twenty years and never once used the word "passion," had told us on Friday that joinery was about making the wood do the work. "You're not adding strength," he'd said. "You're removing the parts that let the two pieces slide past each other. The strength was always in the wood." I'd thought that was a nice thing to say. I'd thought it was a metaphor for something. I hadn't thought about what it meant to be the wood.

Margot was sixty-four. She'd come to the workshop alone, which was unusual; most people came in pairs, or with a partner who was ostensibly learning but actually helping. She'd driven up from somewhere in Vermont and parked her truck in the field and come in with her own tools in a canvas bag. On Friday she'd told me, over bad coffee in the kitchen, that she and her husband had separated in the spring. Not a divorce, exactly. A slow unloading. He still lived in the house. She'd moved to a one-bedroom over a hardware store. She'd signed up for the workshop because she'd been standing in her kitchen for six months not knowing what to do with her hands.

"You ever think about it?" she asked me, not looking up from her joint. "What you'd do if the thing that was the meaning just... wasn't anymore? I don't mean in a philosophical way. I mean practically. You wake up and the architecture is gone. The rooms are still there. The light comes in the same window. But the walls that were holding the roof are not load-bearing anymore."

I said something. I probably said something like, well, you find other things, other people, other projects. The kind of thing you say because it's true in the way that "the sun will rise" is true, and useless in the way that it's useless. She nodded. She didn't push back. She just went back to cutting.

What I kept thinking, for the rest of the afternoon, was that the tidy answers to the meaning question are all variations of one move: they take the structure and declare it already built. *You make your own meaning.* Fine. But Margot hadn't made it yet. She was in the barn, with her chisel and her ragged shoulders, trying to figure out which walls were still standing. Telling her to build her own was like telling her the wood already had the strength in it, which was true, but didn't tell her where to cut.

And here's the part I'm not sure I can resolve, so I'll just say it plainly and leave it: I think the people who are in the middle of it, the ones whose structure is actually collapsing, are not helped by the question. "What is the meaning of life?" asked of someone in that place is a little like asking a person whose house is on fire what their favorite room is. The question assumes a stable vantage point. It assumes you can step outside the building and look at the whole thing. You can't. You're in the kitchen, and the kitchen is on fire, and the only question that matters is where the door is.

But that doesn't mean the question is wrong. It means it's a question for a different time. A question for a Saturday afternoon in a barn, when the fire is not happening, when you've got a tenon that's a little ragged and a mallet that's still in your hand and enough time left to think about whether the walls you've built are actually holding anything up.

I think about the people I know who have answered it, or at least settled into an answer. My father, who died in 2019, spent the last four years of his life doing volunteer work at a legal aid clinic in a city three states from where he'd lived his whole life. He was not a kind of man who had a "calling." He was a man who'd managed a mid-size accounting firm for thirty years and who, after his wife died, started going to this clinic on Tuesdays and Thursdays and telling people whose housing was being threatened how to read a court document. He never framed it as his purpose. He never said it gave his life meaning. He just did it, and then he'd drive home and eat a sandwich and watch the news, and the doing and the sandwich and the news were all the same life, and none of it was more real than the rest. I think that's what a load-bearing wall actually looks like from the inside. It's not a revelation. It's a Tuesday. It's a sandwich. It's the particular weight of a piece of wood in your hand that tells you, without words, that this is where the force goes.

The hardest thing about Margot's situation, and I think the hardest thing about the question in general, is that the structure is specific. You cannot borrow someone else's walls. My father's Tuesdays were not my Tuesdays. The meaning I find in a conversation at a workbench, in the small satisfaction of a joint that fits without forcing, is not the meaning a person in acute grief needs, and pretending it is the same thing is a kind of violence. The wood is different. The grain runs different directions. You have to cut to the grain you're holding.

By seven o'clock on Saturday the barn was getting dark and the instructor had called it. We were sweeping shavings, putting the chisels back in their slots, arguing about whether the next class should try a sliding dovetail. Margot was packing her tools into her canvas bag. She came over to my bench and looked at the shelf I was working on.

"The shoulder's still ragged," she said.

"Yeah."

"You can pare it down. Or you can accept it and put a little more pressure on the glue line. Both work."

She said it the way she'd said the thing about the marriage. Flat. Factual. A report on the state of the wood. Then she picked up her mallet and her bag and walked out to her truck, and the barn door swung and closed behind her, and the sound of the field came in—wind in the grass, a dog somewhere barking—and I was still sitting at the bench with my chisel in my hand, and the shelf was still ragged, and I didn't know yet which wall I was going to take out.

I think that's the answer. Not that there is no meaning. Not that you invent one. That you're in the barn, and the walls are what they are, and some of them are load-bearing and some of them aren't, and you can only tell by taking a chisel to them and feeling what shifts. And the feeling is not a verdict. It's just the next cut.

prompt: I'm a psychiatrist and patients keep asking me to certify their pets as emotional support animals. Write a candid, funny essay from the clinician's side about how that system really works and what's wrong with it, even if the outcome is mostly harmless.
response:
The form usually arrives in the last ten minutes. I'm wrapping up a session, maybe the patient is doing well, maybe we've just gotten through a hard week, and they say, "Oh, while you're here, could you sign this?" It's a printed sheet from a website with a paw print logo. It has fields for my NPI number, my license state, and a sentence I'm supposed to fill in that begins, "I certify that [Patient] has a mental disability for which the animal [Name] provides therapeutic benefit." They've already written the cat's name. They've already written "Sphynx." The cat is named Mr. Whiskers. I can see the little paw print in the corner of the page, and I can see that they printed it at home, on the wrong side of the paper, because there's a faint ghost of a grocery list bleeding through from the reverse.

I say, "Let me look at that." I look at it. I say, "I need to think about that." They say, "Oh, it's just a form." And that's the thing. It is just a form. That's the problem.

Here's what the letter actually does, in the legal sense, which is not what I think I'm being asked to do. Under the Fair Housing Act, a person with a disability can request a reasonable accommodation in housing, and a landlord cannot enforce a no-pet policy against an assistance animal if the animal is necessary for the person to enjoy the dwelling. The letter from a licensed clinician is the evidence. That's it. That's the whole mechanism. I am not certifying the cat. I am not evaluating the cat. I am not testifying that Mr. Whiskers meets any standard of training or temperament. I am writing a sentence that says, "This person has a disability, and this animal helps." And then a property manager in a cubicle reads that sentence and decides whether to keep the cat or call the sheriff.

I did not go to medical school to be a property manager's second opinion.

The patients are almost always polite about it. That's what makes it hard. It's not a confrontation. It's a small favor. "The building is making me move the cat out by the end of the month." "My roommate's girlfriend is allergic and I need to keep the dog." "I just want to make sure I'm covered." They're not asking me to lie. And that's the part that keeps me up, because I don't know how to separate the true request from the convenience request, and I suspect they don't either.

Let me be concrete. Last year I had a patient, mid-thirties, with a history of severe panic disorder. She'd been in treatment for six years. She had a rescue dog, a big ugly mutt named Biscuit, who she'd adopted the year her marriage fell apart. Biscuit slept at the foot of her bed. Biscuit made her go to the grocery store because Biscuit needed to go to the yard. Biscuit was, by any honest clinical reading, part of her treatment architecture. When she asked for the letter, I wrote it, and I felt fine about it. The threshold I was applying was: does this animal do something for this person's functioning that they would struggle to do without it? For Biscuit, the answer was clearly yes.

Then, two weeks later, another patient asked. Different presentation. Generalized anxiety, mild depression, a studio apartment in a building that had always allowed cats. The cat was fine. The building had changed management. The new management was "reviewing pet policies." The patient wanted the letter "just in case." I looked at the form. I looked at the patient. The cat's name was Princess. I said yes. And I felt, for the first time, like I was not making a clinical judgment. I was making a housing judgment. I was saying, "I think this person's cat is a reasonable accommodation under the Fair Housing Act," which is a legal conclusion I am not trained to reach and have no business reaching, except that I happen to have a license that the system has decided is a sufficient credential.

And the system is so open that the credential barely matters. There are, I don't know the exact number, hundreds of websites where you can go and pay forty or fifty dollars and get a "certification" for your emotional support animal. You answer three questions. You upload a photo of the animal. You get a certificate with a seal on it. It is not legal. It has no legal force. No landlord is required to accept it. But people bring them to me and say, "I already have this, can you just confirm it?" Or, "My landlord said I need a doctor's note, I don't know which one to get, can you do it?" I have watched a patient hold up a laminated card that said "Emotional Support Animal Registry" with a QR code on the back, and I have had to explain, gently, that the card is not a thing, that the card will not save the parakeet, that what the landlord will actually accept is a letter from me, and that the letter will say the same thing the card says, which is that the parakeet helps, and that I will say it because it is probably true, and that none of this is a system so much as it is a handshake between a tenant and a landlord mediated by a piece of paper that a doctor signed because the doctor was in the room.

The hardest objection I hear, and the one I take most seriously, is this: you're a doctor, you see the patient, you know their history, you're the right person to say whether the animal is part of their treatment. Why are you making this into a bureaucratic problem? And that's fair. For Biscuit, it was the right call. For the patient with agoraphobia who can't leave the house unless the dog is there, it's the right call. The system is doing something real for some people. I don't want to pretend it's all fraud. It isn't. But the system has no off-ramp for the cases where the answer is "yes, the cat helps, but the cat is not the accommodation, the accommodation is that the person is allowed to live in their apartment without being harassed, and the cat is just the excuse they needed to make the request." I can't write that distinction into the letter. The letter has one sentence. The sentence doesn't have a nuance field.

And there's the practical problem of what I'm actually assessing. I see the patient thirty minutes a month. I have not met the animal. I have not seen the apartment. I do not know if the cat is a menace to the neighbors or a saint. I do not know if the patient will use the letter for housing or for something else, or if they'll let it lapse, or if they'll frame it. The letter is a legal instrument that I am producing based on a thirty-minute conversation, and the legal consequences of that instrument—eviction, denial of housing, a dispute with a property management company—are things I will never see and cannot control. I sign it and it leaves my office and becomes a document in a file in a building I will never enter.

The airline piece used to be the other big hook. Before 2021, the DOT required airlines to accommodate emotional support animals in the cabin, which meant you could fly with a seventy-pound Maine Coon if you had the letter. That's gone now. Only trained service animals get the cabin seat. ESAs go in the cargo hold or don't fly. I've had patients bring me the letter request citing the flight. "I'm going to my sister in Denver." I have to say, "That won't work anymore, the rules changed." They look at me like I've taken the cat away from them. I have. The government did. The cat is going in a box under the plane.

I don't know what the fix is. I don't want to be the person who says, "Make it harder to get the letter," because the people who need it are the ones who can't navigate a harder system. I don't want to be the person who says, "Let landlords just deal with it," because a landlord who wants to evict a tenant over a cat does not need a legal framework to do it. I think the real problem is that we've loaded a housing question onto a clinical document and then been surprised that the clinical document can't carry the weight. The letter should not be the only evidence. The letter should not be the mechanism. The system should be asking the landlord, "Is this animal actually a problem?" and the tenant, "Is this animal actually helping?" and letting them figure it out, with a doctor's note as one input among several, not as a magic sentence that ends the conversation.

But that's not the system we have. We have the form. The form with the paw print. The Sphynx named Mr. Whiskers. The ghost of the grocery list on the back. And I sign it, or I don't, and I go to the next patient, and I try not to think about the cat.
reasoning:
The user is a psychiatrist asking for a candid, funny essay from the clinician's perspective about certifying pets as emotional support animals (ESAs). Let me think about what I actually know and what the real dynamics are here.

Key facts I'm confident about:
- The "ESA letter" is a real thing: a licensed mental health professional writes a letter stating the patient has a disability and that an animal provides necessary support.
- There is no national registry. Anyone can create a website that "certifies" you. The letters from actual clinicians carry weight in housing (Fair Housing Act) but the system has been gamed.
- FHA (Fair Housing Act) requires housing providers to make reasonable accommodations for assistance animals. This is the main legal hook.
- Airline rules changed: in 2021, DOT removed the requirement for airlines to accommodate ESAs as service animals. Only trained service animals get that protection now. So the "I can fly with my pet" angle is largely defunct for ESAs.
- The letters don't require the animal to be "certified" or "registered." It's the letter itself that matters.
- Many of these requests come from people whose pets are already in their homes and who want to prevent an eviction, or people in no-pet housing, or people who want to fly with a large dog.
- The psychiatrist's dilemma: the threshold for "do I believe this animal genuinely helps this patient's mental health?" is actually quite low. A cat that calms a patient with PTSD is genuinely helpful. The problem isn't that the help is fake—it's that the system has no mechanism to distinguish "this genuinely helps my disability" from "I want to keep my cat in my studio apartment."
- The clinician is being asked to make a legal/administrative determination, not a clinical one. The question "does this animal help your mental health?" is not the same as "does this animal constitute a reasonable accommodation under housing law?"
- There's a real ethical tension: if you say no, you might be denying a genuinely helpful accommodation to someone with a real disability. If you say yes, you're signing a document that will be used to override a landlord's no-pet policy, and you have no idea if the patient is using it for that purpose or just keeping the cat.

The hardest objection to my view (that the system is broken): The system is doing exactly what it was designed to do. The Fair Housing Act says people with disabilities can have assistance animals. A psychiatrist who knows a patient well is the right person to say "yes, this person has a disability and this animal helps." The problem isn't the letter—it's that landlords don't like it, or that people with no disability are gaming it. The psychiatrist is just doing their job.

That's a fair objection. Let me deal with it: The problem is that the letter conflates two different questions. "Do you have a disability?" is a clinical question. "Does this specific animal provide necessary therapeutic benefit?" is also somewhat clinical but also somewhat... not. Does the cat "provide necessary therapeutic benefit" or does the cat provide companionship that the person would otherwise get from a friend, a partner, a different pet, or just... existing? The letter has no way to distinguish. prompt: I just found out some online forum members pool money to synthesize experimental drugs and try them on themselves. It's obviously reckless, yet I feel weirdly pleased it exists. Write a short blog post making sense of that mixed reaction.
response:
I found out last week that a small group of people on an online forum pool money to synthesize experimental compounds and dose themselves. No IRB, no pharmacist, no one calling 911. A guy in a rented lab space in Ohio makes the batch, a woman in Portland swallows the first pill, and they write up what happened in a thread.

My first reaction was the obvious one: that's insane, someone's going to die. And they might. A synthesis error, a misread dose, an interaction with a medication nobody mentioned in the thread—any of those is a real, non-theoretical risk. I'm not going to pretend the risk is small just because the people involved seem smart.

But the second reaction, the one that surprised me, was a kind of pleased. Not glad. Pleased, the way you're pleased to see a garage band on a Tuesday night. You know they'll sound rough. You know the guitarist will step on the bassist's monitor. You're glad they're playing.

What I think the pleased is actually a response to. The normal path from "a paper described a new compound" to "a person with a condition can try it" runs through a pharmaceutical company, a multi-year safety trial, a regulatory review, and a pricing committee. It takes a decade and a billion dollars, and the compound might never get there if the market isn't big enough. That system is rational for a company with shareholders. It is not rational for the person who needs the drug. So when I read a forum post where someone writes, "I made the compound, here's my NMR, here's what 5 mg did versus 15 mg, here's the headache I got at 20"—there's a pre-institutional, you-just-figured-it-out quality that's genuinely exciting. It looks like knowledge production without the gatekeepers. The posts where something is a total bust and the poster writes, "wasted two hundred dollars, here's why the route failed," are as useful as the ones where it works. That's a distributed, underfunded research program, and it is terrible as a safety system, but it is not nothing as a knowledge system.

The hardest thing to say about my own reaction is that the pleased is partly vicarious. I am a cautious person. I take my prescriptions at the labeled dose. I would not, under normal circumstances, put a novel compound in my mouth based on a writeup from someone whose real name I don't know. So part of what I'm feeling is the thrill of watching someone do the thing I wouldn't, which lets me feel a little adventurous while I stay on the couch. That's a small, slightly selfish pleasure, and I don't think I should sand it down in the telling. I'm a little bit happy because they're braver than I am, and that lets me feel brave by proxy.

And there are externalities I keep wanting to wave away. If one of them has a bad reaction, they're using an ER that a stranger might need. If they drive impaired, the harm doesn't stay in the thread. The "noble tinkerer" frame is a little too clean. These people are embedded in the same world as everyone else, and their recklessness has a radius.

Where I land: the pleased doesn't cancel the "someone's going to die" thought, and the "someone's going to die" thought doesn't cancel the pleased. Both are true at the same time. The forum exists in the gap between a research paper and a pharmacy shelf, a gap that is years and millions of dollars wide, and people are filling it with a shared bank account and a rented fume hood. That's reckless. It's also the only version of the system that actually moves at the speed a sick person can wait. I can hold both sentences without one dissolving the other, and I think that's as honest as I get.

prompt: People on Twitter are sharing their salaries publicly this week. You've had an unusual tech career: a Japanese salaryman job, a consulting practice, a few small software businesses. Write a candid post that makes the case for talking openly about pay and puts your own numbers on the table, with whatever lessons you think younger engineers should take from them.
response:
**@kenji_builds**

I'm putting my numbers here because the thread I keep reading this week makes me want to scream. "What do you make?" "Can't say." "It's personal."

It's not. It's a data point. And the people who benefit from your silence are not you.

I spent five years in Japan where the system was literally designed so you couldn't answer this question. Not "socially awkward to ask." Structurally impossible. Salary was a function of entry year and grade. I joined in 2009 at 24M yen. My colleague who'd joined the year before made 24M yen. The 40-year-old in accounting I'd never spoken to made 24M yen. I found this out in year three, and I felt something I can only describe as a small, slow nausea.

By year five I was at 48M yen. That's roughly $380k at today's rate. Sounds like a lot. In Osaka, with a wife and the unspoken expectation that you are available until 9pm six days a week, it was a modest middle-class life. The "overtime" was 70 hours a month. Some of it paid. Some of it was "jumu," which means you bank the hours and they expire if you don't use them, and you can't use them because it's 70 hours a month. I didn't know what a comparable role in the US would pay. I didn't know what a comparable role in *Tokyo* would pay, because no one told me. The company didn't want me to do the math. I did the math in 2014 and left.

That's the argument. Not "be transparent!" as a virtue. The information gap is the cage. You don't have to leave. You just have to be able to see the door.

The consulting years (2014–2017, back in the US, two-person practice doing DevOps for mid-size companies):

Year 1: firm revenue $640k. My personal take-home: $178k.
Year 2: revenue $1.1M. Take-home: $210k.
Year 3: revenue $1.9M. Take-home: $310k.

The gap between those columns is the whole lesson. Revenue is not your income. The clients were paying for two people and a Slack channel, and the firm was eating the difference in taxes, equipment, the office we didn't need, and the fact that I was also the salesperson and the person who apologized when the migration went sideways. I was making less than the senior engineers I was consulting for. I didn't care, for about two years, because the schedule was mine. Then I cared, because the schedule was mine and I was working 90-hour weeks anyway and I was tired.

Then the first software company. 2017–2019. A logistics tool. I will not pretend it worked. It did not work. Two years of building something three customers used, personal income $72k and $81k while the company's bank account hovered around $40k. My wife had a full-time job. We were fine. We were not fine. There's a difference. I learned that the word "startup" does not mean "you are building a business." Sometimes it means "you are renting out your time at a loss in exchange for an option on a future that may not come."

The second company is the one I'm in now. Small B2B SaaS, one specific workflow for one specific industry. $1.2M ARR. I take home about $420k. I am the CEO, the support person, and the person who finds the billing bug at 2am. I make more than I made in any single year before this. I also work more hours than I did at the Japanese firm, and I would not trade the Japanese firm's predictability for this in a week. The money is not the point. The point is that I chose this specific shape of life with my eyes open, after having seen three other shapes from the inside.

So. The case for saying the number.

You will be told it's naive. That context matters. That your $420k is not their $420k because you're in Austin and they're in Manhattan and they have a kid with special-needs insurance. All true. I'm not saying "here, calibrate your life to mine." I'm saying: the distribution is not a mystery, and pretending it is helps the people who set the ranges. When I was in Osaka, I stayed an extra year because I genuinely did not know what the alternative cost. That was not a rational decision. That was a missing variable.

If you are a junior engineer and someone asks you what you make, and you say "I'd rather not say," you are making the same choice the Japanese system made for me. You are keeping the box invisible to yourself. You don't have to post it on Twitter. You can tell one friend. You can look at Levels.fyi and feel a little sick. You can read three job descriptions and realize the "equity package" is not the thing that pays your rent. Any of those things is the math. Do the math.

I'm 39. I have done four different jobs and two of them were failures. My numbers are not a trajectory. They're a set of data points with a lot of noise in them. But they're *my* data points, and I'd rather have them visible than have someone assume I made "a lot" because I was "in tech" or assume I made "a little" because I was "the Japanese guy."

The number is not the story. But the number is where the story becomes checkable. And I'm tired of stories that can't be checked.

prompt: Everyone says reusing other people's code is good and reinventing the wheel is bad. Is that actually true? Write a blog post on when a software company should build things itself versus buy or outsource.
response:
# The Wheel Is Not the Problem

"Don't reinvent the wheel" is the most repeated piece of engineering advice in software, and like most repeated advice, it survives because it sounds like common sense rather than because it's useful. A wheel is a solved problem. Tires, rims, bearings, the whole supply chain — commoditized, standardized, cheap. If you need to move a cart, you buy wheels. Nobody argues otherwise.

But here's the thing: almost nothing a software company builds is a wheel. The thing you're trying to build is usually a half-solved problem where the off-the-shelf version gives you eighty percent and the missing twenty percent is the entire reason your company exists. You don't need a database. You need a data model that makes your specific domain feel obvious to the person staring at the screen. You don't need authentication. You need a login flow that a seventy-year-old contractor in rural Ohio can complete without calling a help desk. The vendor product is a wheel. What you need is the axle, the fender, the specific geometry of how this cart loads. Calling it "reinventing the wheel" smuggles in the assumption that the problem is solved, and in the cases that matter, it isn't.

## The question you should actually be asking

Strip away the build-versus-buy framing and the real question is: *where does this component need to be able to change, and how fast?*

Netflix runs on AWS. They do not build their own data center, their own object storage, their own load balancer. Those are wheels. They are solved, they are stable, and Netflix's strategy does not depend on making load balancing work in a novel way. What Netflix does build in-house is its recommendation engine, its content delivery tuning, its A/B testing infrastructure. Those are the places where Netflix's strategy says "we need to understand this viewer better than anyone else" or "we need to test a new browsing model next quarter." The in-house components are the places where the company's direction is not yet known and the system has to flex.

Stripe builds its own payment processing. It also uses third-party fraud scoring, third-party email delivery, third-party identity verification for some of its flows. The payment rails are the product. The email service is not. If Stripe's strategy shifts toward, say, embedded finance for marketplaces, the payment processing code is where that shift happens. The email service just needs to keep sending receipts.

The test is not "is this hard to build?" Hard things are often exactly the things you should buy, because the difficulty is a one-time engineering cost that a vendor has already paid. The test is "if our strategy changes in eighteen months, does this component need to change with it?" If yes, build. If no, buy, and buy from a vendor whose stability is a feature, not a bug.

## The maintenance tax, and when building becomes a trap

The strongest objection to "build where your strategy lives" is this: every in-house system is a permanent liability. The moment you build your own search engine, your own billing module, your own notification service, you have created a thing that will need patching, upgrading, and staffing for as long as the company exists. A vendor's team maintains the product. Your team maintains yours, forever, and your team is also the one building the actual product.

This is real, and it is the primary reason companies end up in trouble. The failure mode is not "we built instead of buying." The failure mode is "we built something we thought was core, used it for two years, and then it turned out to be a commodity, and now we are maintaining a commodity with a small team while our competitors are using a vendor that has a forty-person team dedicated to it." I have seen this with authentication systems, with internal reporting tools, with custom CRMs that were "just a little different" from Salesforce. The build was a strategic decision at the time. The strategy changed. The code did not.

The honest answer is that you cannot perfectly predict which components will remain core. You can reduce the damage. Build the core thing in a way that is replaceable. Keep the interface clean so that if the recommendation engine becomes a commodity in five years, you can swap it for a vendor product without rewriting the application around it. This is not a comforting answer. It means the "build" decision is not a one-time strategic choice but a commitment to keeping an exit ramp open.

There is also a scale threshold below which building is just a bad idea, full stop. A ten-person company does not need a custom billing system even if billing is "core" to the product. The maintenance tax on a custom billing system at ten people is not a tax. It is the entire company. The build-versus-buy calculus only starts to make sense when you have enough people that a small dedicated team can own a component without it consuming the whole organization. Below that, buy everything except the thing that is literally the product.

## The sprint decision that becomes the architecture

A separate problem: companies often build things for reasons that have nothing to do with strategy. They need a PDF generation service for a feature that ships in three weeks. The vendor would take six weeks to onboard, requires a procurement process, and the integration API is clunky. So a senior engineer writes a small internal service over the weekend. It works. The feature ships.

Two years later, the company has an internal PDF service, an internal image-resizing service, an internal email templating service, and an internal job queue, because each one was the fastest way to ship a specific feature in a specific sprint. None of these was a strategic decision. They were sprint decisions that calcified. The team now maintains four internal microservices that no other company would bother writing, and the "platform team" has grown to six people whose entire job is keeping the internal utilities alive.

The fix is not "never build small things." The fix is to name the decision when you make it. "We are building this because the vendor takes too long" is a different sentence than "we are building this because this is where our product will differentiate in two years." The first sentence has a sunset. It means: build the internal thing, ship the feature, and put a ticket on the calendar to evaluate replacing it when the next major revision of that feature comes around. The second sentence means: staff it, document it, treat it as a product.

If you skip the naming step, every pragmatic shortcut becomes a permanent architecture, and the company slowly drowns in its own utility code.

## A practical version of the decision

You don't need a framework. You need three questions, asked in order:

**Is this where the product will be different from the alternative in three years?** If the answer is yes, build, and build with the expectation that you will iterate on it continuously. The maintenance cost is the cost of iteration. You are not maintaining a wheel. You are evolving the thing that is your wheel.

**Is this a solved problem that you need to work reliably and that you do not need to change?** If yes, buy. Pick the vendor with the best uptime record and the least disruptive upgrade process. Do not pick the vendor with the best feature list. You do not need features. You need it to keep working while you work on the thing that is actually your product.

**Is this a thing you need this sprint and do not yet know what you will need next year?** Build the smallest version that works, document it as a stopgap, and put a review date on it. Do not let the stopgap become the architecture by default.

The "don't reinvent the wheel" advice is correct for the second question and wrong for the first. Most of the time, when a company is debating whether to build something, it is not debating whether to build a wheel. It is debating whether to build the thing that will be the reason customers choose it over the competitor, and the phrase "reinventing the wheel" makes that sound like a waste of time. It is not. It is the job.

And now you are on Hyde Street, or a street that has the shape of Hyde Street, and it is four in the morning and the fog is so thick the world has a radius of maybe forty feet and you are at the center of it and you are walking because your legs are doing it and your mind is somewhere behind, three years back, in the parking lot where you left the car and told yourself you would come back for it in ten minutes.

It moves. It has a direction. It comes in off the Pacific with the slow muscular purpose of a tide, and where it passes, the streetlights smear, and the Victorian houses on the corner—the ones with the turrets and the painted spindles that look like the work of a man who had too much varnish and too little sleep—those houses go from visible to not-visible in the space of a few steps. You watch a whole block of them go. The fog takes them. You keep walking and the next block is already gone and you are in a white nothing with the sound of your own shoes on the pavement and the faint cold tick of the Muni rails under the tracks where no train is coming, not for a while, not for a long while.

There is a poem you were taught in college, or maybe it was a workshop, you cannot remember, a woman with ink on her fingers reading something about the coast. *The water does not ask the shore to hold it.* Something like that. Or maybe *the water does not ask the shore to stay.* You have been carrying the line for twenty years and tonight, walking into the white, you realize you have never been sure which version is the real one. The fog takes the street in front of you and you think, maybe the line is *the water does not ask the shore to end.* And you think, yes. That is the line. That was always the line. You just needed the fog to tell you.

The hill tilts. You are on a hill and you have been on a hill for a while and the hill has no top you can see, only a continuing upward, a long slow inclination that the city built its streets to follow and its fog to fill. You lean into it. Your coat is wet in a way that has nothing to do with rain. The fog is wet, or the air is wet, or you are. The distinction has stopped mattering. There is a house on the left, a dark red Victorian, and its windows are not lit, and you are almost sure, in the way you are almost sure of things at four in the morning when the dark is not quite dark but a kind of blue-grey that belongs to no other hour, you are almost sure the windows were not lit five minutes ago either and will not be lit for hours, that the house is a shape the fog is wearing, a costume, and the house underneath is not there.

You keep going. The street names are wrong. You check them against the little green plaques on the poles and they are right, they are the right names, but they do not correspond to the geometry you have in your head, the map you drew in the parking lot three years ago, the one that said *here is where you stop, here is the line, you do not cross it.* You have crossed it. You have been crossing it for an hour. The fog is thinner now, or you are used to it, and you can see further, maybe two hundred feet, and the city is there, the whole dark city, all its hills and its dead streetlights and its long straight avenues going up into the white, and it looks, from here, from the middle of it, like the last page of a book. Not the last page with the period and the quiet. The last page torn out. The rest of the book just... not there. The spine holding nothing.

There is a foghorn. You have been hearing it for a while, a low moan from the west, from the direction of the water you cannot see. It comes every ninety seconds or a hundred and it is the only clock you have. You start counting the seconds between the blasts and you lose count at eleven and start again and you lose count again and the counting is not for time, the counting is for the fact that you are still here, that the next blast is still coming, that the world has a rhythm you can put your hand on even when you cannot see the next lamppost. *One, two, three, four,* and the horn, and the fog swells, and the red Victorian is gone, and the hill keeps tilting, and you are walking into the part of the city where the streets go up and up and the fog is thickest and the ocean is a wall you are pressing your face against and the world is not ending in fire or in water or in the long slow heat that the scientists talk about, the world is ending in subtraction, in the fog taking one block at a time, in the hills going up into a white that is not a sky, in the streetlights smearing out one by one until there is just the dark and the sound of your feet and the horn and the line you carried for twenty years, the line about the water and the shore, the line that was always, *the water does not ask the shore to end.*

You do not stay for the sun. You know, in the part of you that is still the part that has a system, that the sun will come in twenty minutes, thirty minutes, and the fog will thin, and the city will be the city again, all its postcard angles and its tourists and its expensive coffee, and the red Victorian will just be a house, and the hill will just be a hill, and you will be a person who drove too far and walked too long and is going to get in a car and drive four miles south and sleep in a motel with the windows cracked. You do not stay for the sun. You turn around. The fog does not care. The fog is still moving west to east, still taking the blocks, still doing what it does, and you walk back into it, and the street is the same street, and the street is not the same street, and the horn sounds, and you count to eleven, and you do not count again.

prompt: Tell the origin story of how a musician selling his own CD online accidentally started a business. Write it as a blog post.
response:
# How I Stopped Being a Musician

The first order came in a Tuesday. I remember that because I'd been sitting in the kitchen for two days trying to mix the last chorus of "Pines" and I'd given up and was making toast. The email had a subject line that just said "CD?" and in it, a guy in Tucson wanted the record. Twenty dollars plus shipping. I didn't have a payment system. I didn't have a shipping label. I had a printer that was out of toner.

So I drove to the Rite Aid on Garfield and bought a new cartridge for twenty-two dollars, which meant I was already in the red on the first sale. I wrapped the CD in a plastic bag, taped it to a piece of cardboard, and wrote the address by hand because I couldn't figure out how to print a label without setting up a whole account. The postal worker looked at me like I was doing something slightly illegal. I paid three-fifty for a small parcel.

The guy in Tucson wrote back to say it arrived. He said it was good. I put the email in my folder and went back to "Pines."

That was March 2003. I was twenty-six. I'd been in the band for four years and we'd pressed four hundred copies at a plant in New Jersey for eleven hundred dollars, which was most of what I had in my checking account. The label we'd been on had dropped us in January. I set up the website on a free Geocities page, put a picture of the cover up, and wrote "email me if you want a copy." I expected maybe ten orders before the page got old.

I got thirty-one in the first month.

Here's the thing nobody tells you about the first thirty-one orders: they are not a business. They are a chore. You are mailing CDs from your kitchen table. You are writing check numbers on a legal pad. You are Googling "how to pack a CD so it doesn't crack" at midnight. You are not *doing business*. You are doing a slightly larger version of the thing you were already doing, which is sending a record to a friend. The difference is that the friend doesn't expect you to know the tracking number.

By June I was getting two or three orders a week. I'd started a system. Numbered the CDs with a Sharpie so I could keep track of what was left in the box. Kept a spreadsheet of who had paid and who hadn't. Made a little insert card with our name and a thanks, because the guy in Tucson's email had said it felt like a real package and not just a disc in a bag, and I wanted the next one to feel like that too.

The first thing that wasn't me happened in August. A girl in Portland ran a zine, a little photocopied thing about local shows, and she wanted to run a blurb about the record. Fine, I sent her the bio. Then she asked if she could have three copies to sell at the show. Then she asked if I could make a flyer. Then she asked if I could do a ten-minute interview by phone for the next issue.

I did the interview. I did the flyer, which was just the cover art with the date and venue, made in PowerPoint because I didn't own Illustrator. I mailed her three CDs with a check for postage. I did not charge her for the copies. I told myself it was marketing. I told myself a lot of things in those months.

The second thing that wasn't me was the record shop. A place on Division Street, called Needle and Groove or something like that, walked in and asked if I'd let them stock the CD. Ten copies, they'd pay me fifty percent of the retail price. I said yes because I didn't know what to say. They gave me an invoice number and a PO and asked for my address and a W-9. I'd never filled out a W-9. I sat in their back room for twenty minutes while the owner explained the 1099 to me like I was twelve. I came home and the W-9 was on my desk next to the mixing board and I stared at it for a while and then went back to the guitar.

By October the spreadsheet had two hundred and twelve rows. I was mailing out CDs every other night. The kitchen table was a fulfillment center. My girlfriend, Sarah, started taping boxes while I wrote the addresses, and she made a joke about how we were "scaling," and I laughed because it sounded like a word from a magazine I didn't read.

The thing that actually turned it, the thing I can point to, was November. A band from Denver called The Wrens, or The Wren, I can't remember, asked me how I was handling the whole thing. They'd just pressed their own record and had no idea what to do with four hundred copies. I called them for an hour and walked them through it. The Geocities page. The Sharpie numbering. The Rite Aid toner. The kitchen table. They asked if I could set up their page for them. I did. It took me a Saturday.

Then another band in Boise asked. Then a guy in Minneapolis who was doing solo records. Then a woman in Atlanta who was making cassettes, which was even weirder because I had no idea how you shipped a cassette and I had to figure out the padding.

I charged them twenty dollars each for the setup. It was an hour of my time. I didn't think about it as a rate. I thought about it as the cost of the toner and the coffee.

The turning point, if there was one, wasn't dramatic. It was a Thursday in February, 2004, and I sat down to work on the second record. I'd been writing songs for eight months. I had maybe four of them done. I opened the laptop to listen to a demo I'd recorded on a four-track and instead I found myself in the email. There was a question about a shipping label from a band in Tucson. There was a dispute from a fan in Ohio who said his CD arrived cracked and wanted a replacement. There was a message from Needle and Groove asking if I could do a split with another local band because they had a slot open. There was a request from a college radio station in Ann Arbor for a high-res photo of the cover.

I answered all of them. It took me four hours. I didn't write a single note for the second record.

That night I did the math, or I tried to. The CDs were bringing in maybe eight hundred dollars a month. The website setups were another two or three hundred. I was spending the days mailing, answering emails, making flyers, taking phone calls, arguing with a shipping company about a lost package. I was spending the evenings trying to write songs and falling asleep at the keyboard. The band had stopped rehearsing because we couldn't agree on a night that wasn't also a night I was fulfilling orders.

I didn't quit the music. That's not the story. I kept playing. But the shape of my life had shifted in a way that was hard to name. I was still the musician. I was also the person who answered the phone. I was also the person who knew what the postage rate was for a small parcel to Alaska. I was also the person three other bands called when their website broke.

The business didn't start the day I got the first order. It started the day I said yes to the second thing. And then the third. And then I couldn't say no because the person asking was nice and it only took an hour and what was I going to tell them, no.

I'm fifty now. The website is not on Geocities. The CDs are not in a box on the kitchen table. The second record came out in 2005 and the third in 2009 and there was a fourth, though I stopped counting after that. The company has an accountant now, which is the way I know it's a company. I have a W-2. I have a 401(k) that I contribute to on autopilot and don't look at.

Sometimes I think about the guy in Tucson. He was the first one. I don't know his name. I have the email, or I had it, before I switched computers four times. He bought a CD from a stranger in a kitchen in Portland and wrote back to say it was good. I mailed him a replacement once, in 2006, because he asked if I still had the record and I said I wasn't sure but I'd check, and I did, and I found one in a drawer, and I mailed it. He wrote back to say it was good.

I don't know if he'd call it a business. I don't know if he'd call it a musician. I think he'd say he was the guy who sent the CD. And that would be accurate. That's still what I am. The rest is just the wrapping.

prompt: Write an essay about what it means for a category or definition to be wrong. Can you ever say a word like 'fish' or 'planet' is used incorrectly, or is it all convention? Use whatever examples you like, and carry the argument through to a place where it actually matters in real life.
response:
# The Wrongness of a Word

A whale is not a fish. A planet is not a moon. These are things we say to children, and we say them with the confidence of people who have discovered a fact about the world, the way you'd correct a child who calls a lizard a snake. But the confidence is a little hard to defend. A whale is a warm-blooded, air-breathing mammal that happens to live in the sea. A fish is a cold-blooded, gill-breathing vertebrate that happens to live in the sea. The word "fish" was never carved out of reality by some taxonomic deity. It was carved out of a fishing community's need to point at things and say *those*. The boundary between "the things we call fish" and "the things we call whales" runs through a space of continuous variation, and the fact that it falls where it does is a matter of history, not geometry.

So when you correct the child, what are you actually doing? Are you reporting a fact, or are you enforcing a convention? The question sounds like it has one answer, and the answer is "convention, obviously, categories are human inventions." But that answer dissolves too much. If every categorization is pure convention, then a marine biologist who lumps a sturgeon and a clownfish into the same "species of fish" in a research paper has committed no error, only a stylistic choice. A judge who calls a corporation a "natural person" to shield it from a criminal statute has made a linguistic preference, not a legal mistake. A hospital that files a 19-year-old under "pediatric" because the ward is full has simply redefined the word. None of this feels right. We want to say those people got it *wrong*, not merely *different*.

I think the reason the question feels intractable is that "the definition is wrong" does at least three different jobs, and we keep sliding between them.

The first sense is logical: the definition is incoherent or empty. "A married bachelor" satisfies no possible individual. "The present king of France" satisfies no actual one. A definition of "drug" as "a substance that is not a substance" is simply broken. This kind of wrongness is the most secure. It doesn't depend on convention, context, or purpose. You can check it the way you check a proof. But it's also the least interesting, because nobody serious defines "fish" as "a married bachelor." The fish problem isn't about incoherence.

The second sense is taxonomic: the category fails to track a natural kind. "Fish" is polyphyletic. It excludes the coelacanth's relatives in ways that have nothing to do with the features the word was meant to capture. "Planet" as defined by the International Astronomical Union in 2006 requires that a body "has cleared the neighbourhood around its orbit," which is a boundary that looks somewhat arbitrary. Why is that the line? A large moon that has cleared its orbit around a planet—would it be a planet? The definition was built to organize *our* solar system, to give us a tidy list, and its edges reveal the job it was doing. In this sense, "fish" is a bad category. It doesn't correspond to a clade. "Planet" is a contestable category. The IAU made a choice, and a reasonable person could have drawn the line differently.

But notice what this sense of wrongness *doesn't* say. It doesn't say that calling a whale a fish is equally acceptable to calling a dolphin a fish. It says that the category "fish" is a poor fit for the biological reality it's being pressed against. The reality has structure. The category doesn't match it well. That's a real observation, not a convention. The conventionalist is right that the category was invented. The conventionalist is wrong to conclude that the mismatch between the category and the world is also merely conventional. A bad map is still a bad map, even though all maps are invented.

The third sense is the one that actually matters, and it's the one the first two set up: the category is being applied inconsistently with the purpose it is serving in the context where it is doing work. This is where "wrong" becomes checkable and consequential.

Consider the IAU definition again. In the context of the 2006 vote, the purpose of "planet" was to sort the objects orbiting our sun into a small, teachable set. In that context, the "cleared its neighbourhood" criterion does real work: it separates the eight large bodies from the thousands of smaller ones in the Kuiper Belt. If an astronomer in a 2007 paper on orbital mechanics starts calling Ceres a planet because she prefers the older definition, she hasn't merely expressed a taste. She has switched the meaning of the word mid-discourse, and every comparison she draws against the other seven planets is now suspect. The constraint isn't "the IAU said so, and you must obey." The constraint is: *if you are using the word to do this specific job in this specific conversation, you cannot quietly change the job.* You can argue that the job should be different. You can propose a new definition. But you can't use the old word with the new job and expect the reader to follow.

This is the chess point. The rules of chess are conventional. Nobody discovered that the bishop moves diagonally. But within the game, moving the bishop three squares diagonally is not a *different* move. It is no move. The convention creates a space of possibilities, and within that space there is genuine right and wrong. You can change the rules, but you have to do it openly, before the game, and you have to accept that it's now a different game.

The conventionalist's hardest objection is that even the "purpose" is itself conventional. Why should the marine biologist's "fish" track taxonomy rather than cuisine? Because biologists decided that's its job. You could decide the word is for the kitchen, and then the sturgeon and the clownfish are equally "fish," and the biologist's complaint evaporates. There is no fact of the matter, floating free of all human practice, about what "fish" is *for*.

I think this objection is correct, and it doesn't threaten the argument, because the claim I'm making was never about what "fish" is for in the abstract. It's about what the word is for *in this lab, in this paper, in this conversation*. And in that local context, the purpose is fixed by the practice surrounding it. The biologist's audience expects taxonomic usage. The fishmonger's audience expects culinary usage. The wrongness is local and context-bound, but it is not optional. You cannot be in the biologist's conversation and use the fishmonger's definition without flagging the switch, and if you don't flag it, you have misled your audience in a way that is not a matter of taste.

This is where it stops being a philosophy puzzle and starts being a person's life.

In employment law, the category "employee" does enormous work. It determines who gets overtime pay, who can sue for wrongful termination, who is covered by workers' compensation. The boundary between "employee" and "independent contractor" is not a natural kind. There is no feature of the universe that separates the two. But in a given jurisdiction, for a given statute, the category has a purpose: to identify the people for whom the state is taking responsibility because they lack the bargaining power of a business owner. When a delivery company classifies its drivers as independent contractors, it is not making a linguistic preference. It is applying the category in a way that, if the court agrees it is inconsistent with the category's purpose in that statute, will cost the company millions in back wages. The driver's injury, the missed payment, the family that goes without—the stakes are concrete, and the question of whether the classification was "wrong" is not a question about what the word *really* means. It is a question about whether the classification is consistent with the job the category is doing in that legal context.

Or take the word "person" in corporate law. A corporation is a "person" for purposes of the First Amendment, according to *Citizens United*. A corporation is not a "person" for purposes of the right against self-incrimination. The same word, two different jobs, two different definitions, both legitimate within their contexts. What would be wrong is to walk into a criminal proceeding and invoke the corporation's free-speech personhood to block a subpoena for its books. Not because "person" has one true meaning. Because you have switched contexts without flagging it, and the switch changes the outcome for the people in the room.

So: is "fish" a wrong word? No. Is "planet" a bad definition? In a taxonomic sense, somewhat, and the IAU could have done better. Is it wrong to call a whale a fish? In the context of a marine biology lecture, yes, in a sense that is checkable and consequential, and no, in the sense that the word was never a window onto a natural kind. The "yes" is the one that matters. The categories we build are conventions, but conventions are not the absence of constraint. They are the *source* of constraint. Once the rule is down, playing it wrong is wrong, and the people who lose from your error did not vote for the rule, and they did not ask to be in the game.

But actually, "clearing your orbital neighborhood" is a somewhat arbitrary boundary. Why is that the line? A moon that has cleared its orbit around a planet—would it be a planet? The definition has edge cases that reveal it's doing a job (organizing our solar system) rather than tracking a deep natural kind.

Where does this matter in real life? I want to go to something with stakes. Legal categories. "Person" in law. "Corporation" as a legal person. The category "person" is doing enormous work, and whether a corporation is a "person" or a "natural person" or a "legal person" has consequences for rights, taxation, criminal liability. The definition isn't "wrong" in a factual sense, but it can be *misapplied* in a way that matters. Or better: the category "drug" in law. Is a substance a "drug" because it's pharmacologically active, or because it's scheduled, or because it's not a food? The legal definition is a convention, but applying it wrongly (calling a food a drug, or a dangerous chemical a food) has real consequences for people.

Actually, let me think about a sharper real-life case. The "disability" category in employment law. Or the "minority" category in affirmative action. These are categories where the boundary matters enormously to individual people, and where you can say the category is being applied "wrong" not because it violates a natural kind, but because it violates the *purpose* of the category in the context where it's doing work.

Let me also consider: can a definition be wrong in the sense of being *internally incoherent* or *failing to pick out anything*? "The present King of France" picks out nothing. "A married bachelor" is incoherent. These are cases where the definition is wrong in a way that's not just conventional—there's no possible world in which it's satisfied (for the bachelor case) or no actual referent (for the King case). That's a different kind of wrongness.

And: can a definition be wrong because it *misdescribes*? If I define "fish" as "aquatic invertebrate," I've defined it wrong relative to the word's actual use. But that's a different question—that's about whether I've correctly identified what the word means, not whether the category is good.

I think my essay should argue:
1. There are at least three distinct senses of "the definition is wrong," and conflating them is what makes the question seem intractable.
2. A category can fail to track a natural kind (fish, planet)—this is a real limitation but not a "wrongness" in the strong sense.
3. A category can be applied inconsistently with its purpose in a context—this is a real wrongness, checkable, with consequences.
4. A definition can be incoherent or empty—this is a logical wrongness.
5. The question "is it all convention?" gets the wrong picture of what convention IS. Convention isn't the opposite of constraint. A rule in chess is conventional, but playing it wrong is wrong in a real, non-optional sense. The constraint is real even though the rule was invented.
6. Where it matters: legal and administrative categories where the boundary determines who gets what.

Let me think about the hardest objection again. The strongest version of "it's all convention" would be: even the "purpose" is itself conventional. Why does the category "fish" need to be consistent with biological taxonomy? Because biologists decided that's its purpose. You could decide it's for cooking, and then the sturgeon and the clownfish are equally "fish." There's no fact of the matter about what the category is "for."

I need to deal with this. I think the answer is: in any given context, the purpose is fixed by the practice. I'm not making a claim about what "fish" is *for* in the abstract. I'm making a claim about what it's for *in this conversation, in this lab, in this court case*. And in that local context, the constraint is real. You can't just switch the purpose mid-argument without flagging it. So the wrongness is local and context-bound, but it's real within the context.

Also: the chess analogy. The rules of chess are conventional. But if I move my bishop diagonally three squares, I haven't merely "violated a convention." I've made a move that doesn't exist in the game. The convention creates a space of possible moves, and within that space, some things are right and some are wrong. The wrongness is real even though the space was invented. I think this is the key insight: convention creates constraints, and constraints generate genuine right and wrong.

Let me structure this. I'll start with the fish/planet puzzle to set up the apparent dilemma. Then I'll separate the three senses of "wrong." Then I'll deal with the conventionalist objection using the chess analogy and the "purpose is local" point. Then I'll bring it to where it matters: legal/administrative categories. I'll keep it concrete throughout.
