prompt: Give a talk-style essay to an audience of startup founders on whether being genuinely good to users and the world is a sound business strategy, not just a nice sentiment.
response:
# The Precondition, Not the Play

You've been told "be good to your users" is a strategy. I want to push back on that, because I think the framing is making you make bad decisions. Being genuinely good to your users is not a strategy. It is a precondition for a strategy to work. The distinction matters, because a strategy is something you choose to do in a space where you could also do something else. "Charge a premium for a well-designed product" is a strategy. "Go enterprise instead of SMB" is a strategy. "Be good" is not in that category, any more than "don't lie to customers" or "don't serve them malware" is a strategy. Those are the floor. And the reason the floor matters to your P&L is not moral. It's mechanical. Let me show you the mechanism.

When you are genuinely good to your users, three things happen that are very hard to fake, and each one changes your numbers in a way that compounds.

First, churn drops. Not by a little. A SaaS company that actually solves the problem it claims to solve, that doesn't quietly deprecate the feature a customer's workflow depends on, that answers support tickets like a human being rather than a chatbot trained to deflect—those companies see annual churn in the single digits while the median for the category is in the high teens or twenties. Do the math. If your churn is 3 percent instead of 18 percent, you need to replace one in thirty-three customers a year instead of one in five-and-a-half. Your CAC payback period collapses. Your LTV expands by a factor of six. You don't need to "find a wedge" or "land and expand." You just need to keep the people you already have, and that is a dramatically easier problem than the one your peers are solving.

Second, your users become a distribution channel, but only the trustworthy kind. Referral from a satisfied user is not the same as a promo code. When a founder in a niche I know recommended a tool to another founder, the sentence was "I use it, it works, I've been using it for two years." That sentence is doing more acquisition work than a $40,000 Google Ads campaign, because it arrives pre-validated. The customer has already done the due diligence for you. You can't buy that. You can only earn it by being true to what you said for a long enough stretch that the recommendation carries weight. And "long enough" is the part that kills the companies that treat goodness as a marketing phase. You can run a "we care about our community" campaign for a quarter and then quietly raise prices and cut support. The community will notice. The referral channel doesn't just dry up; it inverts. Now the recommendation is "use it, but read the fine print." That is worse than no recommendation.

Third, and this is the one founders underestimate: you can charge more, and the price is credible. A customer paying $200 a month for a tool that they believe is fairly priced, that they believe will still be here in two years, that they believe won't be sold to a data broker, will not shop around at $150. The price signal is doing work that a feature comparison table cannot do. You are selling a relationship with a lower discount rate. The other company's $150 is a number. Your $200 is a number plus a bet on continuity that the customer is willing to underwrite.

Now. I know what you're thinking, and I think it's fair.

Facebook. Uber. The tobacco companies. There are businesses that are, in the plainest sense, not good to their users, that are not good to the world, and that are the most profitable companies on earth. If being good were a sound strategy, those companies would have been outcompeted. So what am I missing?

I'm not missing it. I'm just arguing about what the strategy actually was. Facebook's strategy was not "be good to users." Its strategy was to exploit an information asymmetry: users did not understand that the product was them, and that their data was the product being sold to advertisers. Uber's early strategy was not "give drivers freedom." Its strategy was to classify workers in a way that shifted cost and risk onto them while the platform captured the margin, in a regulatory gap that was closing in real time. These were not goodness strategies. They were concealment strategies. They worked because the user could not see the full transaction. They worked because the regulator had not caught up.

And I will be honest with you about the cost of this argument: some of those companies will outlast their reputations. The asymmetry, once built, is sticky. Network effects don't care about your ethics. A driver who has been on Uber for four years and has a 4.9 rating is not going to switch to a "fairer" platform because of a podcast episode. The window in which a genuinely good competitor can take the market is narrower than the moral argument suggests, and in some markets it may not exist at all. I don't want to oversell this.

But the window is closing, and it is closing faster than those companies' boardrooms model. Regulatory scrutiny is not a sentiment; it is a cost structure. The EU's DMA and GDPR are line items. The speed at which a user can screenshot a terms-of-service change and have it in a congressional hearing is not a sentiment; it is a distribution channel for the company's own bad decisions, and it operates at a speed the company cannot match. The concealment strategy has a half-life. I don't know how long, but I know it's not infinite, and I know the founders who are building on top of it are building on a foundation with a known expiration date.

Now the second half of your question, the "and the world" part, where I have to be more careful.

Being good to the world is a strategy only when it changes what you can offer. If you are a shipping company and your carbon footprint is a real cost to your customers' customers, then reducing it is a product improvement. It shows up in their procurement forms. If you are a restaurant and the people cooking are the product, then treating them well is a product improvement. It shows up in the food. If you are a B2B SaaS company whose entire operation is a server room and a Slack channel, "being good to the world" is mostly a press release, and I will say that plainly because I think you deserve the plainness. It is not a cost center. It is not a strategy. It is a paragraph on your website. And that's fine. You don't owe the world a narrative. You owe your users the three mechanical effects I described, and that is enough.

So what does this mean on Tuesday, when you are making a decision?

It means the question is not "should we be good?" The question is "what is the cheapest way to be less good, and what will it cost me in eighteen months?" Because that is the actual trade-off you are making every time you cut the support team, every time you ship the feature that technically works but breaks the workflow, every time you raise the price and quietly remove the tier a small customer was on. You are not choosing between goodness and profitability. You are choosing between a small, immediate margin gain and a compounding, multi-year margin loss that will not show up in your current quarter's numbers. The goodness is the compounding. The extraction is the interest you're paying on it, and the rate is higher than you think.

You don't need a mission statement. You need to not be the company your users have to explain to their friends. That is the whole strategy. Everything else is tactics.

prompt: Why did prehistoric people all over the world drill holes in each other's skulls, and why did so many survive? And why did the practice die out? Give me your best attempt at solving the mystery.
response:
First, a small correction to the premise. Trepanation—the deliberate removal of a piece of skull—has been found in Europe, the Andes, parts of Africa, and a few other places, but "all over the world" flattens what is really a pattern of independent invention. A Neolithic farmer in France and a Peruvian man two millennia later were not following the same tradition. They were arriving at the same fix for a similar problem with no connection between them. That matters, because it means there is no single mystery to solve. There are several, and they share a logic without sharing a history.

The logic, as best I can reconstruct it, starts with a head injury. A blow from a club, a fall, a piece of stone embedded in the scalp. The person is concussed, bleeding, maybe swelling. To a prehistoric observer, the skull is a box, and what's inside is the seat of the mind. If the box is cracked, the sensible thing is to open it. You don't need a theory of intracranial pressure to think that. You need to watch someone get hit on the head, go still, and die, and then notice that the spot where they were hit is the spot that's worst.

The strongest evidence for this being a medical response rather than a purely spiritual one is where the holes are. In the large Peruvian samples—there are well over a thousand documented trepanned skulls from the Andean region alone—the openings cluster over the areas where a blow would land: the parietal bone, the temporal region, the vertex. If you were performing a rite to release a malevolent spirit, you would probably aim for a symbolically central spot, the crown or the forehead. If you were responding to damage, you go to the damage. The holes go to the damage.

The second piece of evidence is the iteration. In the European Neolithic record, the earliest examples are crude: a broad scrape where someone has rubbed a sharp stone or a flint blade over the bone until it wore through. You can see the parallel grooves. Later examples show a cut, a straight line, and then a section chiseled out. The latest and most refined examples, in the Andes especially, show a clean circular hole, sometimes with the plug of bone still sitting in it, as if the operator could put it back. That progression is not what you see in a ritual. A ritual gets formalized, not refined. A procedure that is killing the patient gets refined. Someone tried scraping, the patient bled out, and the next operator cut more carefully. Someone tried cutting, the edges were ragged and the wound kept reopening, and the next operator made a round hole so the edges would draw together. That is the shape of empirical learning applied to a medical problem.

I should flag the alternative seriously, because it is not crazy. The "release the demon" explanation is what most people give, and it is not nothing. The people doing the drilling had a cosmology in which the skull was a sealed container for something vital, and the act of opening it had to mean something in that cosmology. I think the honest answer is that the medical need and the spiritual framing were the same event, not competing explanations. You drill the hole because the man is swelling and you think the air or the spirit is trapped. The hole is both the treatment and the rite. But the fact that the location tracks the injury, and that the technique improves in a direction that reduces surgical trauma, tells me the medical need was the engine and the spiritual story was the wrapper.

There is a secondary driver I think is real but smaller: epilepsy. A person who seizes repeatedly is a problem in a small community, and a prehistoric observer who has no concept of a misfiring cortex will look for a cause in the body and the most obvious sealed body-part is the skull. Trepanation for what we would call epilepsy is actually attested in Greek and Roman medical writing, so the idea was not limited to the deep past. Some of the holes, especially ones in the absence of any visible trauma to the surrounding bone, are probably for this. But they are a minority of the sample.

Now the question that surprises people: why did they survive? A hole in the skull, made with a stone tool, in an environment without antibiotics, should be a death sentence. The dura is a membrane, the brain is right there, and any pre-antibiotic wound in a warm body is an invitation to sepsis. Yet in the well-studied Peruvian collections, survival rates estimated from the bone healing—smoothed, rounded edges, new bone laid down over the rim—run somewhere around fifty to seventy percent. Some individuals have two or three holes, meaning they lived through the first procedure, recovered, got hit or seized again, and came back. Some show the bone growing almost completely over the opening, which takes months, maybe years.

The key to the survival rate is that the comparison class is wrong if you think of it as "healthy person versus person with a hole." The right comparison is "person with a growing hematoma or a depressed fracture" versus "person with a hole." A lot of these procedures were done on people who were already dying. The swelling was going to kill them in a day or two. The hole let the pressure equalize. They were not saved by the surgery in the way a healthy person is saved by a surgery; they were saved from the specific thing that was going to kill them, at the cost of a wound that, in a well-vascularized scalp, actually closed. The periosteum is tough. A clean circular hole with smooth edges heals by secondary intention, laying down new bone from the rim inward. It is ugly but it works.

Infection was the real killer, and it probably took a third of the patients. But a clean hole is not the same as a ragged crush wound, and the scalp has a blood supply that outperforms most other soft tissues in the body. The ones who survived the first forty-eight hours were usually over the worst of it. And there is a selection effect in the record that I cannot fully quantify: the people who died three days later in the field may have been buried in a way that did not preserve the skull, or in a context we have not excavated, while the ones who lived to be buried in the family grave are the ones whose skulls are in the museum. I am not sure how large that effect is, but it is there.

The third question is why the practice faded, and I think this is where I am least able to give you a clean answer, so I will say what I think and where the thinking gets shaky.

It did not fade uniformly. In the Andes, it continued well into the Inca period. In much of Europe, it thinned out around the transition from the Bronze Age to the Iron Age, but it lingered in the British Isles and in parts of the Alps. So "why did it die out" is really "why did it stop being the default response to a head injury in most places, while persisting in a few?"

My best guess is displacement of the causal story. The practice depended on a specific folk-anatomy: the skull is a sealed box, the mind or the spirit is trapped inside, and if the box is damaged the contents escape or the pressure builds. That model is simple and it is locally true enough to be useful. But it is also a model that can be replaced. Once a medical tradition develops a different account of what a head injury is—humoral imbalance, a blow to the windpipe, a disruption of the blood rather than a breach of the bone—the specific logic that says "you must open the skull" loses its footing. You still treat the injury, but you bleed the patient, you apply a poultice, you pray to a god who lives in the liver. The hole is no longer the obvious move.

In the later historical record, the practice does not disappear so much as it becomes a last resort that is explicitly acknowledged as dangerous. The Greek and Roman writers describe it as a desperate measure, done when the patient is already at the edge. That is a different cultural position from the Neolithic one, where it seems to have been a straightforward response. The knowledge that it could kill you, layered on top of a better (or at least different) theory of what was wrong, made it a step you took only after everything else had failed, and eventually a step you stopped taking at all.

I want to be honest about the limits here. We do not have the prehistoric people's words. We have the holes, the healing, the tools, and the context. The story I have given you—trauma as the trigger, iterative refinement of the technique, survival because the patients were already dying, decline because the explanatory framework shifted—is the story the physical evidence most naturally supports. But "most naturally" is not "necessarily." I cannot rule out that in some communities the dominant motivation was genuinely spiritual, that the injury just happened to be where the spirit was most agitated, and that the refinement of technique was driven by a desire for a cleaner rite rather than a cleaner surgery. The bones do not let me distinguish those two drivers with confidence. What they do let me say is that the practice was widespread, it was learned and improved over generations, a majority of the people who got it lived long enough to be buried properly, and it faded not because the injuries stopped but because the story that made the hole the right answer was told differently.

prompt: You've spent years preaching slow, profitable, bootstrapped growth, and now you're about to take venture capital for a new company. People are shocked. Write a post explaining how you decide whether a business should or shouldn't raise VC.
response:
I've told you, in various posts and talks and one memorable argument at a SaaS conference in 2019, that venture capital is a poison pill. You take it, and the company is no longer yours. You take it, and you can never again decide to stop. You take it, and the only exit is a sale or an IPO, and the only metric that matters is the one that gets you to the next round. I meant every word. I was building a company where the customer bought because our support was good and our tool solved a specific problem we understood. I could fund the next hire from this month's invoices. The market I was in was big enough to support a profitable company and small enough that I didn't need to be the fastest to win. In that world, VC is a luxury you can't afford, because the bill comes due in forced growth.

I am raising $30 million for a new company. Series A, with a lead I respect and two angels who I've worked with before. People in my old community saw the announcement and the reaction was, charitably, "oh." Uncharitably, it was a screenshot with a question mark.

I get the shock. I'd be shocked too, if I didn't already know the answer.

The test I run isn't moral. It isn't "is VC good for the world" or "do I like these investors." It's a question about the shape of the business, and I run it before I talk to a single partner. There are four parts.

**Does the market reward speed, or does it reward fit?**

In my old business, a customer evaluated three vendors, picked the one whose onboarding was clearest, and stayed for six years. Speed was irrelevant. You could be two years late to a feature and the customer would say "thanks, that's great." The competitive dynamic was a slow churn. Whoever was slightly better at serving a specific workflow kept that workflow. In that market, growing 40% a year was more than enough. You didn't need to be the fastest horse. You needed to be the horse that didn't spook.

The new business is different. It's infrastructure. The customer is a mid-size company's engineering team, and the decision is "do we build this in-house or do we buy it from you." The answer depends on whether you exist, whether you're reliable, and whether your competitor exists. If I'm the only one in the market, I win on default. If there are three of us, the customer picks the one with the biggest balance sheet and the longest track record. The window where I can be "the only one" is maybe eighteen months. After that, two other companies with $50 million behind them are hiring the same engineers I want, and the customer's procurement team sees three logos in the G2 category and the game becomes a price and brand war I can't fight with $2 million in the bank.

Speed isn't a nice-to-have here. It's the entire strategy. And you can't bootstrap speed in a market where the competitor's CTO is hiring three people a week.

**Can you fund the gap from revenue?**

This is the one I check against a spreadsheet, not a feeling. In the new business, the enterprise sales cycle is nine months. The first meaningful contract is probably month ten. The product needs to be in a state where it can survive a production workload before that contract closes, and that means a team of eight to ten engineers for at least a year before I see a dollar of revenue. The gap between "we started" and "we're cash-flow positive" is roughly thirty months of burning $1.5 to $2 million a month. I can't fund that. No version of growing "slowly and profitably" gets me there, because there's nothing to be profitable from yet. The revenue doesn't start until the product is done, and the product isn't done in a year.

In the old business, the gap was six weeks. I built a prototype, put it in front of five customers, two said yes, and the money came in before I'd paid for the server. The bootstrap path wasn't an ideology. It was the only path that worked.

**What does the capital actually buy?**

I'm not raising $30 million to "grow faster" in the abstract. I'm raising it to hire twelve engineers in the first ninety days, to put a solutions engineer in front of the five accounts that will define whether this company is real, and to have eighteen months of runway so that if the first product doesn't work, I can find the thing that does without the board calling an emergency meeting in month eight. The money buys a specific set of strategic options that I cannot buy any other way. If I can buy those options another way, I don't raise. I can't.

**Will the obligation to grow destroy the thing I'm trying to build?**

This is the one that kept me up at night, and it's the one that made me take the meeting in the first place. VC money comes with an expectation of 10x in three years. If the business I'm building is a $40 million ARR company in five years, the investors will call that a failure, the board will want to sell, and I'll spend the next three years building a growth machine instead of a good product.

I've thought about this. The market for this infrastructure category is, by my most conservative estimate, a multi-billion-dollar one. The company I'm building, if it works, is not a $40 million company. It's a $500 million company or it's a zero. There is no middle path where I'm profitable, small, and content, and the investors are happy. So the VC-speed obligation and the actual strategic goal are aligned. I don't have to fight the board. I want to be the fastest horse, and the board wants me to be the fastest horse. That alignment is the whole point. It would not have existed in the old business. In the old business, the board would have wanted me to expand into adjacent verticals, and I would have wanted to make the tool I already had better. We would have been at each other's throats.

Now, the objection I can't fully answer.

You can look at all of this and say: you've constructed a clean framework, but the real reason you're taking the money is that you want to build something bigger, and the framework is what you told yourself after the feeling told you what to do. I don't know if that's true. I can't fully separate "this is the right call for this business" from "I am forty-three and I want to build the company I didn't build the first time." I suspect both are true, and that they're not separable. The feeling and the strategy are the same thing, viewed from different angles. I can check the strategy against the spreadsheet and the market, and it holds. I cannot check the feeling. I'll note that here and move on, because pretending I've solved it would be less honest than admitting I haven't.

What I can tell you, concretely, if you're sitting with a business and wondering: run the four tests. If your market rewards fit over speed, if you can fund the gap from revenue, if the capital doesn't buy you a specific strategic option you can't get otherwise, and if the growth obligation would push you away from the product you actually want to make, don't raise. I'd still tell you that. I'd still tell you the poison pill is real. The rules haven't changed. The shape of the business did.

prompt: I spent three months at a programming retreat where beginners improved absurdly fast, and I'm convinced a big part of it was the culture around asking for and giving help. Write a short, punchy blog post about why help matters so much in a community or workplace, aimed at teams that treat questions as interruptions.

Three months at a programming retreat for absolute beginners, and the thing that kept surprising me wasn't the curriculum. It was that a person who'd been debugging a null pointer exception for four days at their job could describe the problem to a peer, get pointed at the actual line, and be moving again in ten minutes. Not because the peer was a genius. Because nobody in that room treated the asking as a small social violation that needed apologizing for.

Here's what I think teams get wrong when they call questions interruptions. They're pricing the cost of the question and ignoring the cost of the silence. The question costs the answerer ten minutes. The silence costs the asker three days of guessing in the wrong direction, building a feature on a foundation that doesn't hold, and then producing a mess that costs the whole team two weeks to untangle during a code review nobody wanted to sit through. The question is the cheap option. It's always been the cheap option. The culture just decided to bill it as expensive.

And I'll grant the real part of the objection, because it's real: if you're three hours into a design decision that depends on holding a whole system in your head, and someone walks up to ask you what a semicolon does, that's a genuine cost. You lost the thread. You're reassembling. The retreat wasn't immune to this. The difference was that the people who needed the semicolon explanation were new, and the people who could give it were between deep work sessions, and the norm was set so that the question came at a time that worked. You can do that in a workplace. You don't need a retreat. You need the team to agree that "I'm in the middle of something, can you wait twenty minutes?" is a complete and acceptable answer, and that the asker doesn't have to feel like they've committed a minor crime by coming back.

There's a second thing that happened in that room that I didn't expect: the answering was also a learning event. The senior-ish volunteers who'd been there a year or two found that explaining why a function wasn't working forced them to articulate a mental model they'd been running on osmosis. They caught their own gaps. The beginner got unstuck, and the helper got sharper. In a team that treats questions as interruptions, you lose both of those returns. You just get a quiet person who's stuck, and a senior who never has to check whether their own understanding is load-bearing.

So what does the shift actually look like? It's not a poster about psychological safety. It's smaller and more mechanical than that. It's that the person who answers gets a visible nod, a "that unblocked me, thank you," something that makes the giving of help a recognized contribution rather than an unpaid tax. It's that a question in standup is met with "okay, what do you think it is?" rather than a sigh. It's that the manager who's supposed to be unblocking people isn't the only person allowed to be unblocking people, because the alternative is a bottleneck with a title.

The beginners I watched leave that retreat could do things they couldn't do when they arrived. A lot of it was practice. But the part that transferred, the part I think they'll still have in five years, is the habit of saying "I don't get this" out loud before the "I don't get this" calcifies into "I'm not the kind of person who gets this." That habit doesn't survive a culture where asking feels like an interruption. And the culture doesn't survive if you keep treating the asking as the problem instead of the solution.

prompt: You just got told in a performance review that you're very good at debugging hard problems, and you didn't used to be. Write a blog post reflecting on what changed.
response:
# The Review Said "You're Good at Debugging Now"

My manager pulled me into a meeting last Tuesday for my mid-year review. We went through the usual items—projects shipped, cross-team work, one thing to improve (scope creep, apparently, because of course). Then she said, almost as an afterthought, "You used to take forever on the nasty bugs. You're actually good at them now." I said thanks. She said, "I mean it. It's a different thing than what you were doing two years ago."

I've been turning over what she meant, because I don't think it's just "I've seen more bugs." Everyone who's been at this longer has seen more bugs. The person two desks over has probably debugged more production incidents than I have. So what's the thing that's different?

I think the most concrete change is that I stopped trying to understand the system and started trying to shrink the problem. Two years ago, when a test failed one time in fifty runs, I would open the codebase, read the relevant files, form a theory, add a log statement, rerun the test suite, and stare at the output. I was doing this in a 400,000-line repository, and my "hypotheses" were basically guesses about which function looked suspicious. I was searching a space the size of the codebase with a flashlight.

Now the first thing I do is build a reproduction. Not a fix. A reproduction. I want a twenty-line program, or a curl command, or a single test with a fixed seed, that fails on its own, without the rest of the system. Last spring I was tracking down a race in our event ordering that only showed up when three specific services were writing to the same topic within a 40-millisecond window. In production it took four hours of load to hit. I spent two days building a load generator that hit that window every 90 seconds. Once I had that, the bug was a missing memory barrier on a shared pointer, and the "debugging" was fifteen minutes of bisecting which of the four functions was touching it. The two days were the hard part. The actual diagnosis was trivial. I didn't realize, until I could do it, that the diagnosis was supposed to be the easy part.

There's a second change that's less technical and more annoying to admit. I used to get attached to my first theory. I'd read the code for ten minutes, think "oh, it's the index," and then spend two days trying to make the index explanation work, reading the query plan, profiling, convincing myself. Last year I thought a p99 latency spike was a slow SQL query. I was wrong. It was connection pool exhaustion three services upstream, and the SQL was just the thing that got blamed because it was the last thing in the stack trace. I caught it because I'd started forcing myself to ask, "what would have to be true for my theory to be wrong?" and then I went and looked for that. The answer was: the query would have to be slow even with a warm cache and a free connection. It wasn't. I'd been reading the query plan and seeing what I expected to see.

I'm less sure about the third thing, and I want to be honest that I'm less sure. I think I've gotten better at noticing the difference between "I've read this code and it's coherent" and "I can predict what happens if I change this variable." The first feeling is common. The second is rare. Early on, I would nod through a 300-line function, feel like I understood it, and then be completely blindsided by the bug that lived in it. Now I can feel the gap. When I can't predict the behavior, I stop pretending I can. I write it down. I ask. I write a test that pins the behavior I *think* it has, and I let the test tell me I'm wrong. I don't know if this is a real skill or just a scar from being wrong a lot, but it changed how I work.

The hardest objection to all of this is that it's just experience wearing a better hat. You debugged a lot, you got faster. The load generator, the disconfirming-evidence step, the "can I predict this" check—those are all just what happens after you've done the thing enough times that the bad versions hurt enough to stop. Maybe. But I don't think the raw count is the whole story. I know people who've been debugging for fifteen years who still do the ten-minute-theory-and-two-day-confirmation loop, because nothing in their process made them notice they were doing it. I think the reflection matters more than the repetition, and that you can get the reflection without the fifteen years, if you write down after each hard bug what actually slowed you down. I started doing that about eighteen months ago. It's not a system. It's a note in a private repo. But the pattern of my own failures is more useful than any debugging guide I've read.

My manager was right that it's a different thing. I'm not smarter than I was. I just stopped doing the thing that made me look smart while making the problem harder.

prompt: Write a blog post about trying to replicate a psychiatry study that claimed a certain snack food could trigger manic episodes, using data from a big reader survey. Be honest about what the data can and can't show.
response:
# I Read 4,200 Survey Responses and Still Can't Tell You Whether Those Crackers Cause Mania

The original study was small. Twenty-three people with bipolar I, mostly young men, kept a food diary for six weeks and logged their mood on a scale. Three of the twenty-three had a manic or hypomanic episode in the three days after eating a particular brand of savory snack crackers. The authors noted the temporal association and used the word "trigger" in the abstract. That word did the work of a controlled trial.

I wanted to see if the association held outside that twenty-three-person room. So I put a survey on the website where I write about mood disorders. The question, in the end, was not "do these crackers trigger mania?" because I had already decided I couldn't ask that and mean it. I asked: How often do you eat [brand]? How often do you have a manic or hypomanic episode in a typical month? Do you notice a change in mood after eating them?

4,217 people answered. 3,402 identified as having a bipolar spectrum diagnosis, the rest were partners, family, or people with other mood conditions who clicked the link and couldn't be bothered to read the exclusion criteria. I ran the analysis on the 3,402.

Here is what the data showed. Among the 3,402, 61 percent reported eating those crackers at least once a week. Of those 61 percent, 14 percent reported a manic or hypomanic episode in the same month they ate the crackers most frequently. That is not a three-day window. That is a month. I don't know which week the crackers came in. I don't know if the episode came before the cracker habit or after. What I can say is that the crackers were present during the month in roughly the same proportion of episodes as in non-episode months: 58 percent of all reported months involved eating them. The association, if there is one, is very weak. Weak enough that I would not be surprised to see it vanish with a slightly different cut of the data.

Here is what the data cannot show. I cannot separate the crackers from the salt, the refined flour, the specific emulsifier, the fact that people tend to eat them at 11 p.m. with a glass of wine while scrolling their phone, the fact that the people who eat them most often are also the people who are least likely to be taking their lithium consistently. I have no control group of people who eat a different cracker. I have no blinding. The people who said "yes, I notice my mood changes after eating them" are the same people who were primed by my survey's very existence to look for a food-mood link. I asked them to pay attention to something. Of course they noticed something.

The hardest objection to my own conclusion is this: maybe the effect is real, and small, and my survey is too noisy to see it. Twenty-three people in a controlled diary study found a signal. Four thousand people in a self-selected internet survey, where half the respondents are eating the crackers on a Tuesday and having an episode on a Saturday for reasons I will never know, might genuinely not have the power to detect a small nudge. The original study's three-out-of-twenty-three is not statistically impressive on its own, but it is a cleaner measurement than my 14 percent of months. I am replacing a small, precise, possibly overfit result with a large, imprecise, probably underpowered one and calling the second result more trustworthy. I am not sure that is fair. I am not sure the original authors are wrong. I am sure the word "trigger" in their abstract was doing more work than their data supported, and I am not sure my data supports less.

What would settle this, or at least narrow it down? A randomized crossover in a moderate sample—say eighty people with bipolar I, alternating two-week blocks of high-cracker-intake and low-cracker-intake, mood rated daily, lithium levels monitored, sleep tracked. That study costs real money and takes a year to recruit. No one is going to do it for a box of crackers. So the question probably stays in the limbo where it is: an anecdote that got published in a journal, a replication that can't refute it, and a mechanism nobody has a strong theory for.

What I actually learned, doing this, is about the word "trigger." In a controlled trial, a trigger is a variable you hold constant and then change and watch the outcome move. In a survey, a trigger is a thing that was present in the same calendar month as the thing you're trying to explain. Those are not the same word. The crackers may be a trigger in the first sense. The crackers are almost certainly not a trigger in the second sense, because they are there all the time, in both the good months and the bad ones, for most of the people in my data. They are the weather. You don't blame the weather for the accident. You blame the ice, the speed, the phone. But "the weather was the weather" is not a very satisfying answer to the person who is in the hospital with a mania and trying to figure out what they can control.

I keep the crackers out of my kitchen now. Not because of the study. Not because of my survey. Because they taste bad and I eat too many of them and I'd rather not be reaching for them at 11 p.m. That is not a finding. It is a person making a small choice. But it is the only kind of finding I was ever going to get from 4,217 strangers telling me what they ate last month.

prompt: Joel Spolsky famously argued that great developers are basically never on the job market, so the resume pile is mostly people nobody else wanted. Write an essay pushing on that claim. Is developer hiring really a 'market for lemons' in Akerlof's sense, and if hiring managers keep saying they can't find good people, what's actually going on?
response:
Joel Spolsky's argument, in its cleanest form, runs like this: the developers you want already have jobs they like, so they aren't applying to your posting. The people who are applying are the ones who've been passed over, or who are between gigs, or who can't seem to get traction anywhere. Your applicant pool is, by construction, negatively selected. Therefore the resume pile is a swamp, and the only way to hire well is to make your company the kind of place great people want to join, then wait for them to come to you.

The practical advice is sound. The economic framing is wrong, and the difference matters because it points to different fixes.

Akerlof's lemons market has a specific mechanism. Sellers know the quality of the car; buyers don't. Rational buyers therefore offer only what an average car is worth. Sellers of good cars refuse that price and exit the market. The pool degrades. The average price drops. More good cars exit. The market collapses toward the bottom. The critical ingredient is that the buyer *cannot verify quality before purchase*, and the price adjusts to the *average* of what's for sale, which drags the whole distribution down.

Developer hiring doesn't work that way, and the reason is that you *can* verify quality, at least to the degree that matters. A good pair-programming session reveals whether someone reasons about tradeoffs or recites patterns. A whiteboard problem reveals whether they push back on a bad premise or just charge at the obvious solution. A reference call reveals whether the person was the one who untangled the mess or the one who asked for help every forty minutes. You don't know everything. You don't know if they'll handle the specific political dynamics of your team, or whether their strengths align with your actual problems. But the information asymmetry is partial and bounded, not the total opacity Akerlof requires. The price mechanism that drives peaches out of the lemon market — the rational buyer offering only average value — doesn't operate in hiring. Companies set comp ranges based on the top of the market and the scope of the role, not on the average quality of last week's applicant pool. Nobody looks at forty resumes and says, "The median is a six, so we'll offer six-level salary." The pool reconstitutes every week. A developer who gets rejected on Tuesday gets a job at a competitor by Friday and is no longer in your pool. There is no cumulative degradation.

So what is the selection effect Spolsky actually identifies, stripped of the lemons machinery? It's simpler and less dramatic than the framing suggests. The top decile of developers, at any given moment, are mostly employed and mostly not looking. That's true of every profession. The active applicant pool is, on average, a few points lower in skill than the employed population. But "a few points lower" is not "a swamp." The pool is full of competent, experienced engineers who are looking for a better problem, a better team, a better city, a better comp package. They are not lemons. They are not people "nobody else wanted." They are people who want something specific and haven't found it yet.

This is where the "we can't find good people" complaint usually unravels. Ask a hiring manager why, and you get a string of answers that have nothing to do with the quality of the applicant pool.

The process is too slow. A great candidate who is actually looking gets three interview loops in the first week. The company that takes four weeks to schedule the second round, that asks for a take-home project that takes an evening, that requires three onsite days before an offer, loses the candidate to the company that made an offer in nine days. The complaint "we can't find good people" is often "we found them and they chose someone else." The people who complain most loudly are frequently the ones whose process is most painful. This is not an information problem. It's a speed problem.

The match is narrower than the search. A company building a compliance-heavy payments platform needs someone who has spent years in that exact regulatory thicket. A "great developer" by any general measure — brilliant systems design, fast at greenfield architecture — may be the wrong person. The job posting says "senior backend engineer, 5+ years." The applicant pool is full of great backend engineers. None of them have spent three years navigating PCI-DSS and SOX audit trails. The hiring manager feels the gap and calls it a quality problem. It's a specificity problem. The candidate exists. They're at a competing payments company. They're not on the job board. But they're not hiding because they're too good to look. They're not looking because their current comp and their kids' school are in the same city.

The bar has moved and nobody noticed. The supply of competent developers has grown substantially since 2012. More CS graduates, a generation of bootcamp-trained engineers who are genuinely productive, international talent entering the US market through remote work. The engineer who was a clear senior hire in 2016 is a solid mid-level in 2024. The hiring manager who calibrated their "great" to 2016 expectations now sees a pool that looks thin. The pool isn't thin. The ruler is wrong.

There is a genuine sense in which Spolsky is right, and it's worth naming because it's the part that survives the pushback. The top of the market is not accessible through a job posting. The people who are extraordinary, who have a track record that speaks for itself, who are building things they care about at companies that treat them well, do not browse Indeed. They get hired through a referral, a conference talk, a GitHub contribution someone noticed, a "hey, I read your blog post from 2019 and we're doing exactly that here." The channel is social and specific, not search-based. If your only hiring channel is a job board and a recruiter, you will never see that person, not because they're a lemon-avoiding peach exiting Akerlof's market, but because they operate in a different information environment than the one your job posting is broadcast into.

The dot-com crash is the cleanest test. In 2001, every "great developer who is never on the market" was on the market. The resume piles that had been "swamps" in 2000 were full of people who had been at Yahoo, at Excite, at a hundred startups that just died. Were they all lemons? Were they all people nobody else wanted? No. They were people whose companies had evaporated. The selection effect Spolsky describes is real but contingent. It depends on a stable labor market in which the best people are attached to employers. Break the stability, and the "swamp" fills with the very people the model says are never looking. Remote work did a smaller version of this in 2021: it broke the geographic monopsony that kept a great developer in Porto from competing for a role in Seattle, and suddenly the "local" applicant pool thinned in a way that had nothing to do with quality.

The lemons framing tempts you into a particular conclusion: that you can't trust the market, that you have to build a brand so strong that peaches come to you. And sure, do that. But the framing also tempts you into a more passive and more pessimistic conclusion: that the market is broken, that the pool is corrupt, that the only rational response is to wait for the rare volunteer. The actual situation is less dramatic. The pool is fine. The process is slow. The match is narrow. The bar has shifted. The top of the market is reachable but only through channels that aren't job boards. Fix those four things and the "can't find good people" complaint mostly goes away, without any appeal to Akerlof.

The user wants me to push on Joel Spolsky's famous claim about developer hiring. Let me think through what I actually think here.

Spolsky's argument (from his blog, around 2008-2010, and the Stack Overflow "Joel Test" era): great developers aren't looking for jobs, so if you're hiring from a resume pile, you're mostly getting people who've been rejected elsewhere. The implication is that traditional hiring is fundamentally broken — you need to attract people rather than search for them.

Is this a "market for lemons" in Akerlof's sense? Akerlof's market for lemons is about asymmetric information: sellers know the quality of the car, buyers don't, so buyers rationally offer only what an average car is worth, which drives good cars out of the market, leaving only lemons. The key mechanism is that quality can't be verified by the buyer before purchase.

Now, does developer hiring actually work this way? Let me think carefully.

The strongest version of Spolsky's claim: truly great developers have options. They're at good companies, they have equity, they're building things they care about. They don't browse job boards. So the people who ARE on the job market are, on average, lower quality. This is a selection effect.

But is it a lemons market? A lemons market requires that the buyer CAN'T distinguish quality. In developer hiring, you CAN distinguish quality, at least to some degree, through interviews, pair programming sessions, take-home projects, references. The problem isn't that you can't tell a great developer from a mediocre one once you're in the room. The problem is that the great ones aren't in the room.

So the failure mode is different from Akerlof. It's not that lemons and peaches are indistinguishable. It's that peaches aren't for sale. The market isn't failing to sort — it's failing to attract. That's a different economic problem. It's closer to a monopsony or a matching problem than a lemons problem.

Now, the hardest objection to my push-back: maybe Spolsky is right and I'm being too charitable. Maybe even with a 4-hour pair programming session, you genuinely cannot distinguish a senior engineer from a mid-level one, because the great things great engineers do (judgment under ambiguity, knowing what NOT to build, political navigation, mentoring) don't show up in a 4-hour window. If that's true, then the lemons framing has more force than I'm giving it.

Let me test this. Can you actually tell? I think you can tell a lot in a good interview. You can see whether someone reasons about tradeoffs or just recites patterns. You can see whether they push back on a bad premise in the problem or just charge at it. You can see whether their questions are sharp. What you CAN'T tell in 4 hours is whether they'll be great at this specific team, in this specific domain, with these specific people. But that's a matching problem, not an information problem.

What about the "hiring managers keep saying they can't find good people" part? What's actually going on?

Several things could be true simultaneously:

1. The selection effect Spolsky describes is real. The top 5-10% of developers are employed and mostly content. The pool of active job seekers is skewed. But this doesn't mean the pool is all lemons. It means the expected value of a random resume is lower than the expected value of the population. That's true but not very actionable — it just means you should spend more time on outreach and employer branding, which everyone already does.

2. The "can't find good people" complaint is often a signal about the hiring process itself. Companies with long, convoluted, multi-round interview processes lose candidates to faster-moving competitors. The great candidates who ARE looking get three offers in a week and take the one that respects their time. The companies that complain most about not finding good people are often the ones whose process is most painful.

3. There's a matching problem that gets mislabeled as a quality problem. A "great" developer for a fintech back-end team is not a "great" developer for a mobile app startup. The person who's extraordinary at distributed systems design may be mediocre at UI engineering. Companies that complain they can't find great people sometimes actually mean they can't find great people who also want to work on their specific, unglamorous problem.

4. The bar is moving. "Great developer" in 2012 meant different things than in 2024. The bar keeps ratcheting up because the supply of competent developers has grown (more CS graduates, more bootcamp grads, more international talent entering the US market via remote work). What was a senior engineer in 2015 is a mid-level in 2024. The complaint "I can't find good people" sometimes means "I can't find people who meet a bar that's shifted up without me noticing."

5. There's a genuine information asymmetry, but it's not the Akerlof kind. It's more that a developer's productivity is context-dependent and slow to reveal. You don't know if someone will be great at your company until 6-12 months in. This creates a genuine search cost problem. But it's not a lemons market because the information eventually arrives, and because references and past-employer checks partially mitigate it.

Now, the concrete cases I should use:

- The 2000 dot-com crash: suddenly every "great" developer was on the market. Companies that had been saying "we can't find good people" suddenly had 200 applicants per role. The pool wasn't all lemons. The pool was full of people who had been employed and content. This directly refutes the strong version of Spolsky's claim.

- Remote work post-2020: the "great developers are never on the market" argument was supposed to be universal. But remote work made it so that a great developer in Porto could compete for a Seattle job. The geographic monopsony broke. Suddenly the market thinned out in a way that had nothing to do with whether great people were "looking."

- The actual mechanism of how great developers get jobs: it's almost always through networks, referrals, "I saw your talk," "I contributed to your open source project." The job board is irrelevant. This supports Spolsky's practical conclusion (don't just post a job) while undermining his economic framing (it's not a lemons market, it's a matching problem where the matching happens through social networks).

Let me think about whether the lemons framing has ANY force. Akerlof's key insight is that the average price adjusts to the average quality, and that adjustment drives out the high-quality sellers. In developer hiring, is there an analogous price adjustment? The "price" is salary + equity + title. If the market for active candidates is skewed toward lower quality, do companies rationally offer less? I don't think this actually happens in the way Akerlof describes. Companies don't look at the resume pile and say "the average quality is 7/10, so we'll offer 7/10 salary." They offer what they think the role is worth, which is set by the top of the market, not the average of the applicant pool. So the price mechanism that drives lemons out of Akerlof's market isn't really operating here.

What IS happening is closer to: companies set a salary range, the people who want that salary range apply, and the distribution of quality among applicants is whatever it is. There's no feedback loop that degrades the pool over time. A developer who gets rejected doesn't become a lemons. They get a job somewhere else and aren't on the market. The pool reconstitutes.

I think the essay should:
1. State Spolsky's claim clearly and steelman it.
2. Show that it's not a lemons market — the mechanism is different. It's a selection/matching problem, not an information problem.
3. Address the hardest version of Spolsky: maybe you can't assess quality in an interview, so it IS an information problem. Push back on this with what you can actually observe.
4. Explain what "can't find good people" usually means in practice: process friction, matching mismatch, moving bars, and the real selection effect (which is real but not as dramatic as Spolsky implies).
5. Use the dot-com crash and remote work as concrete refutations of the strong claim.

Length: this deserves a real essay. Maybe 1000-1400 words. Let me write it with varied sentence length, concrete, no filler. No headers unless it's genuinely a list. I'll use a few short paragraphs for rhythm.

Let me make sure I'm not being too contrarian. Spolsky had a point. The practical advice — invest in employer brand, make it easy to work with you, show up in the community — is good. I should grant that while pushing on the economic framing. The essay should be: "You're right that the resume pile is skewed, but you're wrong about why, and the wrong diagnosis leads to the wrong prescription."

prompt: Congressional voting data gets turned into a left-right scale without anyone telling the algorithm what left and right are. Could something like that work for morality? Write an essay exploring whether you could discover what 'good' means statistically from ordinary life decisions.
response:
# The Axis That Isn't Good

The congressional trick works because policy domains are highly correlated. A representative who votes against the ACA also votes against expanded Medicaid also votes for weaker emissions rules. The correlations are tight enough that one axis captures most of the variance, and the axis looks like a "spectrum" even though the algorithm just found the direction of maximum spread. The labels—liberal, conservative—arrive later, imposed by the people looking at the scatter plot. The structure is real. The meaning is not in the data.

Now suppose you do something analogous with moral life. You track ten thousand people for a year. You record what they tip, whether they return a found wallet, how they handle a disagreement with a coworker, whether they cheat on their taxes, how they speak to their children, what they say in anonymous surveys about helping a stranger in an accident, whether they donate to charity, how they treat service workers. You run a dimensionality reduction. What do you get?

You get something. That's the first thing to concede. People do cluster. A rough first component captures general other-regarding behavior: the people who tip well, return wallets, treat children patiently, donate to charity, and are decent to waiters tend to be the same people. A second axis separates rule-followers from rule-breakers—cheating on taxes, cutting in line, breaking small promises cluster together. A third might separate warmth in close relationships from generosity toward strangers, the person who is tender with family but indifferent to a homeless person versus the person who is cold at home but weeps at a charity gala.

This structure is real and, I think, underexplored. The "character factor"—the first component—probably captures thirty to forty percent of the variance. People who are good in one domain are somewhat more likely to be good in others. The correlation is not trivial. It's the statistical shadow of what Aristotle meant by the unity of the virtues, except weaker: the virtues are correlated, not identical.

But "correlated" is doing enormous work in that sentence, and the gap between what you have and what you wanted is where the whole question lives.

## The direction problem

In the congressional case, once you find the axis, you can at least describe its endpoints in substantive terms. One end is "wants to regulate business, raise taxes, expand the safety net." The other is "wants to deregulate, cut taxes, shrink the state." You can evaluate those positions. You can disagree about which is better, but the disagreement is about the world, not about a label. The axis has content.

The moral axis has no content in the same way. Its endpoints are something like "more other-regarding, more rule-following, more consistent" and "less so." But which end is *good*? The data cannot tell you. A psychopath who is perfectly consistent in their self-interest sits at one extreme. A saint sits at the other. The algorithm finds the axis. It cannot say which direction points toward the good. To say "the other-regarding end is the good end" is to import a moral theory that the statistics never contained. You have not discovered what good means. You have discovered that people vary along a dimension, and then you have *decided* that one direction is the one you care about.

This is Hume's is-ought gap, but the statistical framing makes it worse rather than better, because the visual of a clean axis tempts you into thinking the structure is doing the normative work. The axis looks like it's *telling* you something. It's only telling you that people differ.

## The observability problem

Even if you solved the direction problem, the data is systematically biased toward what is measurable, and what is measurable in moral life is the least interesting part. You can observe that someone tipped twenty percent. You cannot observe that they did it because they resented the waiter and wanted to prove to themselves that they were not petty. You can observe that someone returned a wallet. You cannot observe that they did it out of a cold, calculating belief that being known as honest is useful, rather than out of any regard for the person whose wallet it was. The moral content is in the intention, the motive, the private evaluation, and those are precisely the things that do not appear in a dataset.

The most morally significant decisions are also the ones least visible. What you do when no one is watching. What you choose to care about. Whether you let a grudge fester for twenty years or let it go. Whether you grieve someone properly or perform grief for an audience. These are not in the tipping data. They are not in the wallet data. They are not in the anonymous survey, because the anonymous survey captures what you *say* you would do, which is a different thing from what you would do, and a different thing again from what you would do if you knew the consequences would be private and permanent.

A statistical model of observable behavior is a model of the *performance* of morality, not of morality itself. And the performance can be decoupled from the thing. A person can perform goodness flawlessly—tip well, donate generously, speak kindly, return wallets—and be, in the private architecture of their judgments and loyalties, a person you would not trust with your life. The data would score them at the top of the axis. They would not be a good person.

## The hardest objection, honestly

The strongest case for the statistical approach is this: maybe the private stuff—the intentions, the motives, the unobservable judgments—is not what morality actually *is*. Maybe morality is just the pattern of behavior, and the talk of "really caring" versus "performing care" is a philosophical luxury that doesn't map onto anything in the world. On this view, if someone tips well, donates generously, treats their children patiently, and is kind to strangers, they *are* a good person, full stop, and the question "but do they *really* mean it?" is incoherent, a demand for an extra ingredient that the recipe doesn't call for.

This is a defensible position, and I should not dismiss it. If you hold it, then the statistical approach works almost as well as the congressional one. You find the axis, you label the other-regarding end "good" (and this label is not arbitrary, because you have a substantive theory that goodness *is* other-regarding behavior), and you have a working moral scale.

But I don't hold that position, and I think most people don't, even when they don't notice. The reason is that we actually do distinguish, in practice, between the person who is kind because they are kind and the person who is kind because they are managing a reputation. We call the first one good and the second one something else—strategic, or cold, or performing. We are not being incoherent. We are tracking something real. And that something real is not in the behavioral data.

## What you could actually do

None of this means the data is useless. It means the question "can you discover what good means statistically?" has the wrong shape. You cannot discover *what good means* from the data, because meaning is not a thing the data contains. But you can do something genuinely valuable that is easier to state than to execute.

You can map the *structure* of moral variation. You can find out that honesty about money correlates with honesty about relationships at about 0.5, but that treatment of animals correlates with treatment of coworkers at only 0.2. You can find out that the "character factor" is strongest in domains involving direct interpersonal contact and weakest in domains involving abstract principles. You can find out that people who are generous with their time are not necessarily generous with their money, and that this is a stable individual difference, not noise. You can find out that moral consistency breaks down in specific, predictable ways: under time pressure, in domains where the beneficiary is anonymous, in situations where the cost to the self is high.

This is interesting. It is not "what good means." It is "how moral life is organized, where it holds together, and where it comes apart." The congressional analogy, properly understood, gives you this: the structure of the policy space, the axes along which disagreement runs, the places where the left-right sorting breaks down (trade policy, immigration, gun control, where the one-axis model visibly fails). That is useful knowledge. It is not the same as discovering what the axis *means*, and pretending it is would be a mistake.

You can build the map. You cannot read the destination off the map.

prompt: You co-founded Y Combinator and have advised hundreds of startups through it. Write a reflective essay on what you've learned from your own 'users', the founders you've funded.
response:
I used to think the job of a YC partner was to teach founders things. You sit across from a twenty-three-year-old who has just built a half-finished website and you say, "Here, you need to do X, and also Y, and also you should probably charge money." The first year or two I ran batches that way, and it felt productive. I was dispensing wisdom. The founders were students.

Then I noticed the founders who didn't listen to me were the ones doing better.

Not all of them. Not consistently. But enough of them, and enough of the time, that I had to reckon with the possibility that I was not the teacher. I was the one who needed to be taught, and the students were three weeks into a batch and already three months ahead of me in their specific domain.

The most important thing they taught me is that the distance between your mental model and the world is not a bug in the startup process. It is the startup process. I had internalized the Silicon Valley story of the brilliant founder who sees the future and builds it. The plan is right; execution is the challenge. But what I kept watching, batch after batch, was founders whose plans were wrong in ways they could not have predicted, and who survived by discovering the error fast and changing direction. Not pivoting, which implies a single dramatic turn. Just a continuous, slightly uncomfortable correction. The company they ended up building was not the company they pitched me in the demo. It was a cousin. A distant, unrecognizable cousin.

A concrete case: I remember a batch where a team came in with a social network for professional plumbers. The idea was fine, the team was fine, the market was real. By the end of the batch they had dropped the social network. They had built a scheduling tool. They had discovered, by talking to forty plumbers, that plumbers did not want to be social with each other. They wanted to know which of their six vans was at which job. The scheduling tool became the company. The social network was a wrong answer to a real question, and the real question turned out to be different from the one they had asked.

I could have told them that in week one. I couldn't. Nobody could have. The only way to learn it was to talk to the plumbers, and the only way to know which plumbers to talk to was to talk to the first ten and realize you were asking the wrong question.

This is where I have to be honest with myself about what I'm claiming. I am looking at the companies that worked and extracting a pattern from them. I am not looking at the three hundred startups that talked to forty plumbers, built the scheduling tool, and died anyway because the market was too small or the unit economics were broken or the founders stopped getting along. Survivorship bias is not a trivial concern. When I say "the founders taught me that your mental model is wrong and you have to keep correcting it," I am selecting for the ones whose corrections happened to land. The ones whose corrections kept landing on other wrong answers are not writing essays. They are working at a mid-size SaaS company now, and they do not think of their time in YC as a learning experience. They think of it as a gap in their résumé.

So what I learned is real but it is partial. It is the shape of the terrain, not the map. I know the terrain is rougher and more unknown than I expected. I do not know which of the rough patches are fatal.

What else they taught me, and this one I am more confident about, is that experience is mostly a liability in the early stages. I used to value the founder who had been a VP of product at a big company, because I assumed that experience was information. It is not. It is a set of habits. The VP of product at a big company knows how products get made at a big company: committees, roadmaps, stakeholder management, a nine-month development cycle. None of that transfers. The twenty-two-year-old who has never shipped anything but has an obsession with a specific problem and the willingness to cold-email two hundred people before the product exists—that person is free in a way the VP is not. The VP has to unlearn. The twenty-two-year-old has nothing to unlearn, only to learn.

I say this with the caveat that I have funded plenty of experienced founders who did well and plenty of young ones who did not. The correlation is real but weak. What I actually mean, when I say experience is a liability, is that it is a liability in the specific window where you are trying to find out what the product is. Once you have that, experience becomes an asset. The learning phase and the scaling phase require different people, and most founders are one or the other, not both. YC is for the first phase. That is a useful thing to know about yourself, even if it is not flattering.

The thing about "do things that don't scale" that I did not fully appreciate for a while: it is not a tactic. It is not a growth hack you deploy in month three and then automate away. It is how you find out what the product is. When Airbnb's founders went door to door in New York and personally took photographs of the apartments, they were not doing a marketing stunt. They were doing research. The photos were the product, at that stage. The website was the product, at that stage. The experience of a stranger showing up at your apartment and you making sure the sheets are clean and the coffee works and the lockbox code is posted on the door—that was the product, and you can only learn it by doing it, by hand, for a few dozen people. The moment you automate it, you lose the signal. You no longer know what the user actually experienced. You know what your code executed.

I think this is the core of what the founders taught me, and it is humbling. I have a degree from Harvard. I have written code for twenty years. I have run a company. And the twenty-year-old in the batch who has been cold-emailing for six weeks knows more about her user than I do, because she has been in the contact with the user and I have not. My knowledge is secondhand. Hers is not. The only advantage I have is that I have seen enough batches to recognize the shape of what she is doing. I can say, "That sounds like the pattern that worked for the last three companies in your space," and she can say, "Yeah, but ours is different because of X," and she is right, because she is in the contact.

I have stopped trying to be the person with the answers. The job is to be the person who notices when a founder is not in contact with their users. When the founder is talking about the product in the abstract, in the language of the business plan, rather than in the specific, slightly embarrassing details of what a real human did with the thing last Tuesday. When I hear "we're building a platform" in week two, I know the founder is not in contact. When I hear "the thing broke and the user called me and I had to get up at two in the morning to fix it," I know the founder is in contact, and I leave them alone.

That is most of what I learned. The rest is a list of specific, ungeneralizable things: that the first revenue is more important than the first user, that a founder who has a day job is not as urgent, that the best technical founders are often the ones who are most embarrassed about the design, that a team that argues in public and works in private is healthier than one that works in public and argues in private, that the batch matters more than the funding, that you cannot invest in a person, you can only invest in a person doing a specific thing at a specific time, and that the thing and the time will change, and that is not a failure of the investment thesis, that is the investment thesis.

I do not have a clean lesson. I have a set of corrections to my own assumptions, and the corrections are still coming. Every batch, a few founders do something I have not seen before, and it works, and I am stuck for a language to describe it, and I write it down badly in my notes, and the next batch someone else does it differently and my notes are wrong again. That is the job, I think. Not to accumulate wisdom. To keep being wrong in new ways, and to be the person in the room who notices that the founder is right and the note is wrong.
