prompt: Write a personal essay, in the first person, about why someone who has experienced harassment at work might stay silent about it for years, and why the usual media coverage of these stories can make that silence worse rather than better.
response:
The first thing I want to say is that the silence was not one decision. It was not a moment where I sat down and chose not to speak, the way the news stories make it sound, where someone finally *finds the courage*. It was a thousand small not-speaking moments, each one easier than the last, because by the time the hundredth one came, the not-speaking had become the shape of my life. I had a job. I had a rent. I had a story I told myself about what had happened, and the story was manageable, and the story was that it was just how the office was, just how he was, just a bad year.

The harassment, if I'm going to be precise about it, was not one thing. There was the comment, made in the break room, about my weight, delivered with a laugh that included me so I couldn't be the person who was laughed at. There was the way my name was left off the cc line on client emails for three months while my work was credited to a man who had done none of it. There was the Tuesday when he told me, in front of the whole floor, to "maybe try being a little less intense" after I'd asked a question about a number that didn't add up. There was the time I came back from lunch and my desk had been moved to the corner by the supply closet, no explanation, no apology, just a new chair to sit in. None of these are a firing offense. None of them are a thing you can put in an email to HR with the subject line "complaint." You can't say *I was harassed* and then list "moved desk" and "tone of voice" and "left off an email thread" and expect a process to engage. The system is built for the thing that happened to the woman in the article, the thing with the photograph and the specific sentence and the date. My thing was a weather. It just rained.

So I stayed. Not because I was brave enough to stay, but because the cost of leaving was visible and the cost of staying was invisible. If I left, I had to explain why, and the explanation would be the list, and the list would have to be true, and I would have to say out loud, to a recruiter, to my mother, to my own reflection, that this is what it was. If I stayed, I just had to keep going to the corner desk. The invisible cost is the one you pay in your own body, in the half-second delay before you walk into the office, in the way you start editing your own sentences before you say them. No one sees that. No one can file it.

I left after four years. Not because of a dramatic confrontation. Because I got a call from a friend at another firm. And the silence continued, because the practical reason for it was gone and the emotional architecture was still standing. You don't just stop being quiet because you quit. You built the quiet. It has load-bearing walls.

And then, a year later, a story like mine broke in the paper. A woman, same industry, similar complaints, and the coverage was exactly what I expected it to be. Her name in the headline. A photograph of her, composed, looking slightly past the camera. The paragraph that said she had "remained silent for years before finally speaking out." The paragraph that named him. The paragraph that said he had resigned. The paragraph that said she hoped no one else would have to go through what she went through. I read it in about four minutes. I felt, I don't know, *relocated*. Like someone had taken a photograph of a room I'd been living in and put it in a magazine, and the room in the photograph had a window, and my room didn't.

Because the structure of the story is a dam breaking. The silence is the buildup, the pressure, the thing that makes the eventual speech feel earned. And the speech is the point. The resolution. The thing the reader is there for. What the structure can't hold is the four years of not-speaking that don't lead anywhere. It can't hold the fact that I never did speak. That I left and got a different job and went home and cooked dinner and the thing I had been doing for four years, the thing that was the whole plot of my internal life, just *stopped being relevant* because I wasn't there anymore. There is no article about that. There is no "she finally spoke" because she didn't. There is no villain who resigned. There is no photograph. And so the story doesn't exist, and the person doesn't exist, and the four years are just gone, unaccounted for, like a gap in a tax record.

The coverage also does something else, and this is the part I'm still working through. It makes the silence look like a moral state. *She found the courage to speak out.* Which means the not-speaking was a lack of courage. Which means I was, for four years, a person who was not brave enough. And I want to push back on that, because I think it's wrong, and I think it's wrong in a way that matters. The silence was a calculation. The calculation was: if I speak, I lose the job, or I lose the job and also lose the credibility, or I lose the job and the person I'm speaking against is my boss and my boss's boss and the client who pays for the work and the two people on my team who will have to decide, in a meeting, whether to believe me or believe the person with the title. The calculation was rational. It was the same calculation you make about whether to cross a street in front of traffic. You don't call the person who waits for the light a coward. You don't say *she finally found the courage to cross*.

But here's the part I'm not sure about, and I'll say it because I think it's true: I don't think the coverage is malicious. I don't think the journalists are trying to make other people's silence worse. I think they are writing the story they can write, with the access they have, in the format the format requires, and the format requires a before and an after, a name and a face, a thing that happened and a thing that was done about it. The story I have, the story that is actually true, doesn't fit the format. And so I stay in the corner of the supply closet, and the woman with the window gets the photograph, and both of us are real, and only one of us gets to be in the paper.

I don't know what the better coverage looks like. I don't know if it exists. I know that the sentence "she had remained silent for years" is doing a lot of work in those articles, and I know that the work it's doing is making the years look like a prequel, a setup, a thing that only matters because of the thing that came after. The years are not a setup. The years are the thing. And no one writes an article about the years, because the years have no photograph, no name to put in the headline, no resignation to confirm. The years are just a person sitting in a corner desk, editing their own sentences, going to work.

prompt: Write a blog post encouraging engineers to tell a colleague's manager when that colleague does great work, especially as a way to support people from underrepresented groups. Cover when it matters, how to do it well, and what can go wrong.
response:
# The Jira Ticket Doesn't Say Her Name

A senior engineer spends three weeks untangling a database migration that two previous attempts had failed. She finds the real problem: a trigger that fires in a different order than the schema implies, causing a silent data loss only under a specific write pattern. She writes up the fix, opens the PR, adds a comment explaining the trigger ordering. The PR gets merged. The migration runs. The data is correct. No one files a bug. No one posts in the team channel saying "the migration is fixed." The work is done, and the evidence of who did it is a commit message and a code review thread that forty people will never open.

Six months later, she's in a promotion cycle. Her manager, assembling the packet, writes: "Contributed to the data platform migration effort." That's accurate. It's also useless. The manager genuinely cannot reconstruct the specific, hard, senior-level judgment call because no one routed that information to them. The manager was in standup, in the architecture review for a different project, in a vendor call. The manager did not see the trigger. The manager did not read the PR comment. The information existed, lived in one person's head for a few days, and then degraded into a vague sense that "the migration thing got sorted."

This is not a story about a bad manager. It's a story about how work becomes invisible in an organization that produces more output than any single person can track. And the invisibility is not evenly distributed. It lands harder on the person who is new, or who is the only one of their background on the team, or whose style of working is less performative than the team's default. The person who speaks up in the architecture review gets their name attached to the decision. The person who stays after the meeting to write the design doc that makes the decision implementable gets "the doc was in the shared drive."

So: tell the manager. Not in a way that turns you into a career manager for your colleague. Just: "Hey, I wanted to flag that the way [name] handled [specific thing] was the difference between us shipping this month and being two months behind. The approach to [X] was genuinely the hard part and they saw it before the rest of us did." Two sentences. An email, or a line in the next 1:1 you have with the manager, or a note in the manager's calendar invite for the next team sync. Low effort. The information arrives.

## The objection you're about to raise

If the colleague is a woman, or Black, or South Asian, or trans, and you are none of those things, the instinct is: why is *you* the one doing this? Doesn't that make me the gatekeeper of their visibility? Doesn't it imply they can't walk into their own manager's office and say "I did X and it was hard and here's why"? Doesn't it put me in a position of power I didn't ask for, where I get to decide which of their contributions are worth mentioning?

These are real concerns and they're not dismissible. If you only ever do this for the underrepresented person on the team and never for the five other engineers, you have made their identity the reason their work is noticed, and that is worse than the invisibility you were trying to correct. If you do it in a way that requires the colleague to manage your kindness—asking permission, thanking you, performing gratitude in front of the manager—you have created a small social tax that the majority-group engineers don't pay.

Here's how I think about it, and I'll grant that it's a judgment call where reasonable people land differently. The manager is not a malfeasance. The manager is a person with eight direct reports and a quarterly planning cycle who cannot read every PR and attend every pair-programming session. The information about what was hard and who figured it out is genuinely lost unless someone transmits it. You saw it. You're in the room. The transmission costs you ninety seconds. The colleague who is in the room and says nothing is not choosing silence out of pride; they're doing the same thing everyone does, which is assume the system will catch it. The system does not catch it. The trigger-ordering insight does not file its own promotion evidence.

So you transmit it. And you transmit it for the other engineers too. You tell the manager that Dave's on-call rotation fix saved the team from a 3 a.m. page. You tell the manager that Priya's code review caught the off-by-one in the billing calculator before it hit production. You do it for everyone, and you find that you do it more for the person whose contributions are less visible by default, and that asymmetry is the correction, not the problem. You don't narrate the asymmetry. You don't say "I wanted to make sure you knew about Sam's work because I don't think you've seen as much of it as you should." You just say what Sam did and why it was hard.

## When it matters

It matters most in a narrow window: the four to eight weeks before a promotion review, a transfer decision, or a budget conversation where headcount and individual contributions get weighed. In that window, the manager is actively assembling evidence and is open to it. A specific, well-timed observation lands in the packet. The same observation sent three months after the decision is a nice email that changes nothing.

It matters when the work leaves no artifact. Refactoring. Code review. The on-call fix that prevented an incident you will never hear about because the incident didn't happen. The design doc that made the project possible but got a "👍" in the thread. These are the contributions that a manager's memory does not retain, because they produced no visible output. The only record is the people who were in the room. You were in the room.

It matters when the person is in their first year or two. The manager is building a model of who this person is from a small sample. One clear data point—"this person made a senior-level architectural call in the payment service redesign"—does more work in a small sample than it would in a large one. After three years, the track record carries itself. In month seven, it doesn't.

It matters when the manager and the colleague are far enough apart in background that the manager's default mental image of "a senior engineer doing senior work" does not include the colleague. This is the uncomfortable one, and I want to be careful here because I'm describing a pattern I've seen and heard described, not a universal. But if the manager has been promoted from a path where the people around them at senior level looked, talked, and worked like them, and the colleague does not, the manager's recognition of senior-level judgment may be calibrated to a different presentation style. Your note says, in effect: "This person is operating at the level I'm describing. Here is the specific evidence." You are not grading them. You are providing the data point the manager doesn't have.

## How to do it without making it weird

Be specific to the point of being almost embarrassing. "Great work on the project" is noise. "The way they modeled the idempotency keys for the webhook retries meant we didn't have to rewrite the consumer when we added the second provider" is a sentence a manager can put in a document. If you can't name the specific thing, you probably don't have a strong enough observation to transmit, and that's fine. Don't pad.

Do it directly. A line in your next 1:1 with the manager, or a short email, or a note in the shared team doc if that's where the manager looks. Not in the team Slack channel where it becomes a public performance and the colleague is now the subject of a group conversation about their achievements. Not in a meeting where you have to narrate your own intention. Private, brief, done.

Don't ask permission first. "Hey, can I mention your migration work to [manager]?" puts the colleague in the position of managing your gesture. They now have to say yes graciously or no without seeming ungrateful, and they have to think about what you'll say. Just do it. If they find out and ask, "Oh, I mentioned the trigger thing to [manager] because I wanted them to have it for the review." Done. No ceremony.

Be accurate about collaboration. If you pair-programmed and the key insight was theirs, say "they saw the trigger ordering before I did and that was the unlock." If it was genuinely joint, say "we worked through it together and the indexing approach was the hard part." A manager will notice if you're inflating, and an inflated note from you costs the colleague more credibility than the silence.

Do it for people you don't particularly like. This is the test that separates the correction from the friendship. If you only flag the work of the person you enjoy talking to at lunch, you are being a friend, and the friend is also, coincidentally, the underrepresented person, and the effect is the same patronizing dynamic you were trying to avoid. The person you find difficult to work with, whose work is nonetheless good, deserves the transmission too. If you can't bring yourself to do it, that tells you something about your own biases that is worth sitting with, but the colleague doesn't owe you the time to work through it.

## What can go wrong

You misattribute. You're fairly sure Sam had the idea for the connection pooling fix, but it was actually a 40-minute whiteboard session and the other person drew the diagram. You tell the manager it was Sam's approach. Sam's manager now has a false data point. The other person's contribution is erased. This is recoverable but annoying, and it erodes trust if the other person finds out you took the credit for the idea. When you're not sure, say "Sam and I worked through it" and describe the technical content. You don't have to solve authorship.

You overstate. "The best implementation I've seen in my career" is not true and the manager knows it's not true and now they discount the next three things you say. Calibrate. "This was the hardest part of the project and they handled it cleanly" is strong and true. You don't need superlatives. The specificity does the work.

You create a dependency. You tell the manager about Sam's work, and Sam is gratified, and the next time Sam does good work, Sam waits to see if you'll mention it. You leave the team in eighteen months. The transmission channel is gone. Sam has not learned to do it themselves because you were doing it for them. This is the real long-term cost, and I don't have a clean answer. I think the answer is that the system should not require a third-party transmitter for a person's own work to be visible, and until it doesn't, you do the transmitting, and you accept that you are a stopgap, not a solution. You can also, at some natural point, say "I mentioned the migration thing to [manager] by the way, and I think it's worth you bringing it up in your next 1:1 too, in your own words." You route the information and you also model the act. Both.

The manager reads it as you taking proximity credit. "I was part of the migration team" is the subtext of "I wanted to tell you about Sam's work on the migration." If you and the colleague were both in the room, the manager may file it under "the people who were there" rather than "the person who did the hard part." This is less likely to happen if you are specific about the technical content and less likely if you are not the colleague's peer but a slightly different role—someone on the adjacent team, a contractor, the person from the platform group who was on the call. If you are a direct peer, the ambiguity is harder to avoid, and you just have to be precise about what the person did versus what the team did.

## What this is not

This is not the fix. If the promotion criteria are vague, if the review process requires a manager's narrative and the manager's narrative is shaped by who they have lunch with, if the team has one underrepresented person and the onboarding assumed they would find their own mentors, then your ninety-second email is a bandage on a structural problem. You are routing one piece of information through a channel that should not be necessary. The right system makes the information visible without a third party. The pull request has a description. The design doc has a byline. The on-call log names the person who fixed the page. The promotion evidence is assembled from artifacts, not from a manager's hazy recollection of who said what in a meeting four months ago.

Until that system exists, the information is lost, and the loss is not random. You saw it. You can say it. It costs you nothing and it costs the person you're helping nothing except a small, manageable awkwardness that fades in a week. The trigger-ordering insight deserves to be in the record. The only way it gets there is if someone types the sentence.

The user wants a blog post about engineers telling a colleague's manager when that colleague does great work, framed as a way to support underrepresented groups. Let me think about what I actually believe here and what the hardest objections are.

My main idea: In engineering organizations, credit flows upward and laterally through informal channels that are not neutral. People who are socially proximate to the majority group get their good work noticed by default. People who are not get their work absorbed into the team's output without individual attribution. Telling a manager "hey, [person] did X and it was excellent" is a small, low-cost intervention that corrects a real information asymmetry. It's not charity. It's routing information that would otherwise be lost.

Hardest objection: This is patronizing. It puts the white man / majority-group person in the position of granting visibility to the underrepresented person. It implies the underrepresented person can't advocate for themselves. It also risks the underrepresented person feeling like their work was only noticed because someone else flagged it, rather than on its own merits. And it can create a weird dynamic where the person you're "helping" feels indebted to you or feels like you're managing their career.

Second objection: It's not actually that simple. Sometimes the work genuinely IS team work, and singling out one person is a misattribution. Sometimes the manager already knows. Sometimes the "great work" is just doing the job well, and flagging every competent contribution is noise.

Third objection: The structural problem isn't solved by individual acts of notice. If the promotion process is broken, if the review system is broken, if the team composition is broken, one kind email doesn't fix it. So is this just a feel-good gesture that lets the organization off the hook?

Let me deal with these honestly. I think the patronizing objection is the strongest one and I need to take it seriously rather than wave it away. But I think it's overstated in practice. The alternative to a colleague saying "hey, Sam's implementation of the retry logic was genuinely clever and saved us from a whole class of edge cases" is that Sam's name appears on a Jira ticket and that's the extent of its visibility. The manager who's reviewing 8 direct reports for a promotion cycle doesn't have time to go read every ticket. The information IS lost unless someone routes it. That's not patronage; it's the same thing a manager does when they say "I noticed the latency dropped 40% after the cache change" in a 1:1. You're just doing it for someone else's 1:1.

But I need to be honest about when it's NOT appropriate. If you do it only for the underrepresented person and not for the other six people on the team, you've made it about their identity, which is exactly the patronizing move. If you do it for everyone, it's just good collegial behavior and the diversity framing is incidental. I think the honest answer is: do it for everyone, and yes, you'll find yourself doing it more for the person whose work is less visible by default, and that's fine, that's the correction.

Concrete cases I can use:
- The person who did the hard migration that nobody sees because it "just worked" (the failure case is invisible)
- The person who stayed late to unblock a teammate's PR and the teammate never mentions it
- The person who wrote the design doc that made the whole project possible but got a "nice doc" in the thread
- The promotion packet problem: managers write "contributed to project X" and the specific person's contribution to X is vague

What can go wrong:
- You misattribute. You think Sam did the clever thing but actually it was a pair-programming session and the other person had the idea. You've now put a false credit on Sam's record.
- You overstate. It was good work, not "the best I've seen in five years." The manager discounts you.
- You create a dependency. Sam starts waiting for you to vouch for them. You leave the team. Now who routes the information?
- The manager reads it as you taking credit by association. "I'm telling you about Sam's work" can land as "I was involved in Sam's work."
- You do it in a way that makes Sam the subject of a conversation about their identity. "I wanted you to know, Sam is our only woman on the team and she's doing great work" — no. Never that.

How to do it well:
- Be specific. Not "great work" but "the way they handled the race condition in the connection pool was the difference between us shipping on Friday and being two weeks late."
- Do it to the manager directly, not in a group setting where it becomes a performance.
- Do it for people you don't particularly like. That's the test. If you only flag the work of the person you're friendly with, you're just being a friend, not correcting a visibility gap.
- Don't ask the person's permission first. "Hey, can I tell your manager about the thing you did?" is awkward and puts them in a position of having to manage your kindness. Just do it, and if they ask why, say "I wanted to make sure they knew."
- But do check: if the work was genuinely collaborative, say "Sam and I worked through this together and their approach to the indexing was the key insight." Be accurate.

When it matters most:
- Before a promotion cycle. The manager is assembling evidence. Your specific recollection, sent in a timely way, is usable. Three months after the decision, it's a nice email.
- When the work is invisible by its nature. Infrastructure, refactoring, code review, on-call fixes that prevented an incident. These leave no artifact. The only record is someone's memory.
- When the person is new. First 6-12 months, they don't have a track record. The manager is pattern-matching on a small sample. One data point of "this person is excellent at Y" carries more weight when the sample is small.
- When the person is in a team or org where they're the only one like them and the manager is not from that background. The manager's default mental model of "who is a senior engineer" may not include this person. Your note says "this person is operating at senior level, here's the evidence."

Let me think about structure. This is a blog post. It should feel like a person talking to other engineers. Not a listicle. But the user asked for "when it matters, how to do it well, and what can go wrong" so there's a natural three-part structure. I'll use headers for those three sections but keep the prose within them flowing.

I'll open with the concrete problem (information loss, not malice) and the patronizing objection up front, deal with it, then move into the three sections. I'll close with something that doesn't feel like a summary — maybe the honest limit of what this does.

prompt: There's a stereotype that the left thinks problems are social and fixable while the right thinks they're biological and fixed. Write an essay arguing about whether that gets things backwards.
response:
The stereotype presents a clean axis: the left sees a social world that can be redesigned, the right sees a biological world that must be endured. If you take that axis seriously, you expect the left to be optimistic and the right to be fatalistic, the left to say "we can build it better" and the right to say "this is just how things are." But when you look at what each side actually says about specific problems, the axis doesn't hold. What holds is a different disagreement, and it's a harder one to pin down.

Consider the left's account of poverty. The standard formulation is that poverty is not a failure of individual effort but a product of structure: underfunded schools, the legacy of redlining, the collapse of manufacturing, the criminal-justice pipeline. None of these is a trait a person carries in their cells. They are arrangements of institutions, and arrangements can in principle be rearranged. So far the stereotype fits. But follow the logic a step further. If the structure is the cause, then the person inside the structure is not really an agent. The poor person is not choosing to be poor any more than a river is choosing to flow downhill. The system does the causing. And now ask: can the system be fixed? The left's answer is always collective action, structural change, the reallocation of resources at the scale of the nation or the global economy. But the system is so large, so many-sided, so riddled with countervailing interests, that no single actor can grip it and reshape it. The fixability is real in the same way that the fixability of climate is real: true in the abstract, and in practice a matter of waiting for some convergence of political will that may not come in any given person's lifetime. The individual inside the system is not free to fix it. The left has located the cause outside the individual and then discovered that the thing outside the individual is too big for the individual to move. The result is a determinism that is social in its content but fixed in its structure. You are what the system made you, and the system is not something you can reach.

Now take the right's account of the same problem, or of something adjacent to it, like crime in a distressed neighborhood. The right does not say "these people are biologically criminal." That was Cesare Lombroso, and it is not what a Republican legislator says on the floor. What the right says is that the family has broken down, that the community has lost its norms, that no one is enforcing standards of behavior on the young. These are social facts. The family is an institution, not a gene. The norms are learned, not inherited. And the right's prescription is that these institutions can be repaired: get the father back in the house, get the church back on the corner, get the community back to a place where it can look a teenager in the eye and say no. This is a social diagnosis with a social fix, and it is, crucially, a fix that an individual or a small group can actually execute. You cannot un-redline a neighborhood. You can sit down at the kitchen table and talk to your kid.

So the left's account is social but effectively unfixed for the person it describes, and the right's account is social and fixable at the scale of the person it describes. The stereotype has the fixability reversed.

You can test this with a second case. The left says race is a social construct, not a biological fact. This is the left's most explicitly anti-essentialist claim, and it is the one the stereotype points to as proof that the left sees everything as malleable. But notice what the construct is made of. It is made of the system. Race is not a free-floating idea that any person can pick up and put down. It is the trace of centuries of specific institutional decisions: who was allowed to own land, who was counted as three-fifths of a person, who was bused to which school, who was surveilled by which police department. You can reframe the category. You can argue about whether it should be called race or something else. But you cannot reach into the past and unmake the accumulation. The left's anti-essentialism applies to the label, not to the history under the label. The structure that produced the category is treated as bedrock. The right, by contrast, is happy to treat the category as real and fixed—race is race, the family is the family, the individual is the individual—but then treats the institutions above it as artifacts that can be reformed. The right's fixed thing is the person. The left's fixed thing is the system.

The hardest objection to all this is straightforward, and I should not skip it. The left does not, in its own self-understanding, treat the system as fixed. The whole project of the left is that the system was made by people and can be unmade by people. Capitalism is not a law of nature. The state is not a natural entity. The left's entire epistemology is anti-essentialist, and to say "the system is the bedrock" is to say something the left would deny. And the right does have a genuinely fixed element: the claim that human nature is constant, that the drive to dominate and the drive to form a pair-bond are not cultural inventions but evolutionary facts. That is biology, and it is fixed, and the stereotype is pointing at something real when it names it.

I think the objection is fair as far as it goes, but it describes the rhetoric, not the operative model. The left says the system is changeable while building its moral framework on the premise that the individual is a product of the system and therefore not fully responsible for what the system has made of them. The right says human nature is fixed while building its policy framework on the premise that the individual is autonomous enough to be held responsible for every outcome that nature did not directly compel. In practice, the left's "you are the product of your conditions" and the right's "you are the product of your choices" are the same sentence with the arrow pointed in a different direction. Both remove the person from the center of the explanation. Both make the person an effect rather than a cause. The difference is where the cause is located, and whether the thing doing the causing is something the person can reach.

That is the actual disagreement, and it is not the one the stereotype names. The left and the right both have a fixed thing and a fixable thing. They just disagree about which is which. The left has fixed the system and freed the category. The right has fixed the individual and freed the institution. And the practical consequence of that disagreement is not optimism versus fatalism. It is a disagreement about who gets to be an agent. On the left, the system is the agent and the person is the object. On the right, the person is the agent and the institution is the object. Both arrangements leave someone without hands.
reasoning:
The user wants an essay arguing whether the stereotype—that the left sees problems as social and fixable while the right sees them as biological and fixed—gets things backwards. Let me think about what I actually think here.

The stereotype: Left = social construction, malleable, we can redesign institutions. Right = biological, fixed, you can't change human nature.

Does it get things backwards? Let me think about concrete cases.

Left claims that are actually "fixed" in character:
- The left's insistence on the permanence of certain social structures. Actually, no, that's not quite right.
- The left's reliance on systemic analysis that treats systems as so totalizing that individual agency is minimized. "You can't blame the individual, the system is the problem." This is a kind of determinism. If the system determines outcomes, then individuals within the system are not truly agents. This is structurally similar to "biology determines you."
- The left's view of, say, poverty: it's not that people are lazy (a biological/individual trait) but that the system is broken. But if the system is broken and you can't change the system (because it's too large, too interconnected, too many stakeholders), then the individual is stuck. The fixability claim becomes theoretical.
- Intersectionality at its most developed: your identity is a product of intersecting systems of oppression. You cannot step outside the system to critique it. This is a kind of determinism.

Right claims that are actually "social and fixable":
- The right's emphasis on institutions: family, church, community, local government. "Fix the family and you fix the society." This is a social, institutional fix.
- The right's view of crime: it's not that criminals are biologically criminal (the right actually rejects the "born criminal" idea more than the left does in practice). It's that broken communities, absent fathers, weak norms produce crime. Fix the norms, fix the crime. That's social and fixable.
- The right's view of education: it's not that poor kids are genetically less capable. It's that the school system is broken, that parents aren't involved, that the community doesn't enforce standards. Fix those social conditions.
- The right's view of the economy: it's not that some people are naturally fit to be rich and others naturally fit to be poor. It's that regulations, incentives, and institutions shape outcomes. Change the rules, change the outcomes.

Wait, but the left also says this. The left also says "change the institutions." So where's the actual difference?

Let me think harder. The real difference might be:

The left tends to think the social environment is so totalizing that it determines who you are. Your race, class, gender, sexuality—these are not choices, they are conditions imposed on you by a system. You are what the system makes you. The system is the cause. This is a form of determinism that is social in content but fixed in structure. You can't opt out of your race. You can't opt out of your class (really). The system is the biology.

The right tends to think the individual is more autonomous than the left admits. You can choose your family, your religion, your work ethic, your community. The social environment matters, but you are not wholly constituted by it. You have agency within it. This is a form of individualism that is more "fixed" in the sense that it locates the problem in the individual's choices rather than the system.

So: the left says "the system made you this way" (social content, deterministic structure). The right says "you made yourself this way" (individual content, but also a kind of fixedness—you are responsible, you are what you chose to be).

Actually, I think the inversion is this: the left's social determinism is functionally the same as the right's biological determinism. Both say "you are what you are, and the cause is outside your individual will." The left says the cause is the system. The right says the cause is your nature (or your choices, which once made, fix you). The left says you can't be blamed because the system did it. The right says you can't be excused because you chose it (or you are what you are).

But wait—the right doesn't always say "you are what you are." The right says "you can do better." That's the fixable part. The right's message is: the family is broken, but you can fix it. The community has fallen apart, but you can rebuild it. The individual is autonomous and can choose.

And the left's message is: the system is broken, but it's so totalizing that no individual can fix it. Only collective action, only restructuring the whole. But the whole is so complex, so many interests, so deeply entrenched, that it may never be fixed. The left's fixability is aspirational in a way the right's is not.

Hmm, but I should test this. Is it true that the left is more deterministic? Consider: the left says "privilege is a product of the system, not of individual merit." The right says "merit is real, you earned your position." The left's view: your position is fixed by the system (you were born into a class, a race). The right's view: your position is fixed by your effort and talent. Both are determinist in a sense. But the right's determinism is agentive (you chose your effort), while the left's is non-agentive (the system assigned your position).

The hardest objection to my view: the left is not really deterministic. The left explicitly says "nothing is fixed, everything is constructed, and construction can be deconstructed." The left's entire epistemology is anti-essentialist. Race is a social construct, not a biological fact. Gender is a performance, not a nature. This is the opposite of fixedness.

And the right is not really about individual agency. The right's actual policy positions often assume fixed hierarchies: some countries are naturally more capable of democracy, some people are naturally more entrepreneurial, the family structure is natural and unchanging. The right's "natural order" is a fixed structure.

So maybe the stereotype is right after all? The left says "race is constructed, we can reconstruct it." The right says "the family is natural, you can't change it."

But I think there's a subtlety. The left's anti-essentialism applies to the categories of identity (race, gender) but not to the system. The system is the one fixed thing. The left will say "race is a social construct" but not "the capitalist system is a social construct that we chose and could unchoose." The system is the bedrock. The categories on top of it are flexible, but the structure is not. You can reframe race, but you can't reframe the fact that capital accumulates.

The right's "natural" applies to the individual and the family, not to the state. The right says "the family is natural, the individual is autonomous" but "the state is a necessary evil, a machine that will be captured by special interests." The state is not natural, it's a constructed artifact, and it's fixable (or rather, it needs to be constrained). The right's fixability is institutional: fix the rules, constrain the state, protect the family.

So the real picture: both sides have a fixed thing and a fixable thing, but they disagree about which is which.

Left: the system is fixed (or at least, so large and complex that it's effectively fixed for any individual). Identity categories within the system are constructed and negotiable.
Right: the individual and the family are fixed (natural, autonomous). The state and its institutions are constructed and can be reformed.

The stereotype says: left = all fixable, right = all fixed. The truth is: both are half-fixed and half-fixable, just in different places.

But the question asks whether it gets things "backwards." I think the more interesting claim is that it's not so much backwards as flattened. The stereotype presents a spectrum (social↔biological, fixable↔fixed) when the actual structure is a disagreement about what is the unit of analysis and what is the bedrock.

Let me also think about a concrete case: obesity. The left says obesity is a product of food deserts, marketing to children, the structure of the food industry, stress from poverty. Fix the system, fix the obesity. The right says obesity is a product of individual choices, lack of discipline, the breakdown of the family meal. Fix the individual, fix the obesity. 

The left's account is social but it's also deterministic: if the food system causes obesity, then the obese person is a victim of the system, not an agent. The right's account is individual but it's also fixable: you can choose to eat differently, you can restore the family meal. 

Here the stereotype holds: left = social + (implicitly) you can't really fix it at the individual level because the system is too big. Right = individual + fixable (just choose differently).

But another concrete case: the gender pay gap. The left says it's structural—discrimination in hiring, the "motherhood penalty," occupational segregation produced by socialization. Fix the structures. The right says it's partly preference—women choose different careers, negotiate differently, prioritize different things

prompt: I've just finished Infinite Jest and I'm still puzzled. Write a long, funny, opinionated review for people who've read it (spoilers fine) that tries to say what the book is actually about and how its structure relates to that.
response:
# The Book Is the Film

You finished it. Congratulations. You are now one of the people who spent seven hundred pages flipping forward and backward through footnotes about the etymology of "entertainment" and the treatment protocols for opiate withdrawal and the specific biomechanics of a tennis player's knee, and you put the book down on a nightstand and stared at the ceiling for a while because you were not sure what you had just read. You are not sure what you have just read because the book did not let you read it the way you read books. It made you lose your place. It made you skip a footnote and then realize you needed it three pages later. It made you read a two-hundred-page appendix about a tennis injury and come back to the main text and forget what chapter you were in. It made you do the thing you do when you're trying to follow a conversation at a party where everyone is talking over each other: you flip back, you check, you lose the thread, you start the paragraph over.

And I think that's not a flaw. I think that's the whole argument.

The obvious reading, the one that shows up in every "what is Infinite Jest about" essay, is that it's about entertainment as a form of social control. The O.V. is going to broadcast a film so perfect that everyone who sees it will stop wanting anything else and die of a kind of terminal boredom. This is a warning about Netflix. This is a warning about the attention economy. The book is doing something more specific and more mean than "entertainment is bad." It's staging the experience of being unable to follow the narrative you're supposed to be following, and it's arguing that this experience is the same experience as being an addict, as being in a marriage where the other person is always three sentences ahead of you, as being in a treatment program where everyone speaks in the vocabulary of the program and you can't find your own words underneath it.

He wrote a book that *is* disorienting, and the content of that disorientation is: this is what it feels like. This is what it feels like to be Hal, who can't get a full sentence out, who speaks in fragments and jokes and deflections. This is what it feels like to be in the ENFAT group where you're trying to say the thing that's actually wrong with you and someone interrupts with a program phrase and you lose your thread and you have to start over. This is what it feels like to be in a relationship with your mother, who is trying to explain to you what the O.V. is doing and keeps getting lost in the explanation and has to start over and you are nine years old and you are already not tracking.

You put the book down and you're in the parking lot and you're not performing anymore and the true thing is small and it's specific and it's about a body and it's about a person you love who can't say the thing directly and you can't say the thing directly and you're both in the same room and the room is full of other people who are also failing at it and the failure is the only honest thing in the building and the only thing that isn't a product or a procedure or a joke.

prompt: Suppose a city wanted to become the next Silicon Valley. Is that even possible, and if so what would it really take? Write an essay working out what actually causes a technology hub to form.
response:
The city council member who floats the idea of "becoming the next Silicon Valley" is usually picturing a specific sequence: attract a university program, build an incubator, offer tax breaks, host a conference, and the startups will arrive. This sequence is backwards. It describes what is present in a hub, not what causes one to form. The question is not what Silicon Valley has but why it is there and not in, say, Albuquerque, where Sandia National Laboratories has employed thousands of physicists and engineers for decades.

The honest answer to the first part of the question—whether it's even possible—is yes, with a major caveat. A city can become a significant technology center. It has happened repeatedly: Boston became a biotech hub, Tel Aviv became a cybersecurity hub, Bangalore became a software services and now some genuine innovation center. What a city cannot do, with high probability, is displace Silicon Valley in the domains where Silicon Valley is already the center of gravity. The reason is not some mystical "culture of innovation" but a specific kind of network effect that compounds over decades.

Consider what actually happens when a machine-learning researcher in 2024 is deciding where to work. The obvious answer is that they go where the other machine-learning researchers are, because that is where the collaborations, the job interviews, the informal conversations at a conference that lead to a startup, and the pool of potential co-founders all are. This is not a policy choice. It is a density problem. Once a field reaches a critical mass in one location, the marginal benefit of being there exceeds the marginal benefit of being anywhere else, and the equilibrium is self-reinforcing. You can offer a researcher in Raleigh a 30 percent salary premium to come to Raleigh, and some will come. You will not get the person who is deciding between a job at a lab in Mountain View and one in Raleigh, because the Mountain View job comes with a network that the Raleigh job does not, and the network is worth more than the 30 percent.

This is why the "replicate Silicon Valley" projects have mostly failed in the way people expect. China built Haidian in Beijing and Zhangjiang in Shanghai with enormous capital, top universities, and explicit government direction. They produced a large number of companies, many of which are genuinely impressive. But the entrepreneurial structure is different: the state is a closer partner and a closer threat, the capital is more patient and more directed, and the failure rate is lower because the state absorbs some of the downside. It is a different kind of hub, and it is real, but it is not a copy. Singapore, which has capital, world-class universities, and a government that has been explicitly trying to build a tech ecosystem for thirty years, has a presence in fintech and some AI but not the dense cluster of independent, venture-backed, founder-led companies that defines a Silicon Valley. The physical infrastructure was built. The ecosystem did not follow, because the ecosystem is not the buildings.

What actually caused the Bay Area to become what it is is a chain of specific historical events that cannot be re-run in a different zip code. In the 1940s and 50s, the federal government concentrated aerospace and defense R&D in the southern California and northern California corridor because of existing industrial bases and proximity to the Pacific. Lockheed, Northrop, Douglas, and a set of university research institutes (Stanford, Caltech, the University of California system) were already there. This created a deep pool of engineers who were used to building complex systems and who were paid well. In the 1960s, a subset of these engineers, influenced by the counterculture that was simultaneously exploding in the same geography, started leaving large firms to build smaller things: integrated circuits at Fairchild, then at Intel, then at a hundred smaller companies. The venture capital industry emerged in part because there were enough technically literate wealthy people in the area to evaluate a pitch for a company making a new kind of memory chip, and in part because the legal and tax structures in California at the time made it relatively easy to form and dissolve a corporation. The personal computer, the internet, and each subsequent wave reinforced the cluster.

The important thing to notice is that none of this was planned. No city council in Palo Alto in 1968 voted to create a hub. The hub emerged from the interaction of a specific labor pool, a specific cultural moment, a specific set of legal structures, and a specific pattern of federal procurement, in a specific geography, at a specific time. You cannot order that again.

This does not mean a city cannot build a technology center. It means it has to be honest about what it is building. The conditions that are genuinely replicable are: a strong university or set of universities in the relevant field, a legal environment that makes it fast and cheap to form a company and to let it die, a pool of early-stage capital that is local and willing to take on the specific risk profile of the relevant industry, and a critical mass of practitioners in the field. These are necessary. They are not sufficient, because they do not by themselves create the density of informal interaction that makes a hub a hub.

The conditions that are not replicable by policy are the cultural ones, and these are the ones that get hand-waved in every "innovation strategy" document. The Bay Area in the 1970s was a place where an engineer could be a little weird, where leaving a prestigious job to work in a garage was not a career-ending scandal but a reasonable bet, where the social currency was what you had built rather than your title. This was not a policy. It was the product of a population that was largely recent, that had not yet settled into the hierarchies of an older city, and that was being shaped by a specific moment in American culture. You can import the engineers. You cannot import the fact that their grandparents were not also engineers in the same city, which is what makes the social norms more permissive about risk.

The practical implication for a city that wants a technology hub is that it should aim for a domain where the existing center of gravity is not yet locked in. If you want to be the next Silicon Valley in consumer software, you are almost certainly too late; the network effect is too deep. If the emerging field is, say, the software and tooling layer for quantum computing, or the biotech applications of CRISPR, or the systems layer for autonomous infrastructure, and the field is young enough that no single geography has yet captured the critical mass, then a city with the right universities, the right legal environment, and a deliberate effort to concentrate practitioners in one physical area has a real shot. The shot is not "become Silicon Valley." The shot is "become the place where this particular thing happens, the way Boston is the place where biotech happens."

There is one more consideration that the city council member should weigh, and it is a cost, not a benefit. The technology hub that forms in your city will, in most cases, be a hub of extraction as much as creation. The companies that succeed there will not stay in your city. They will move their headquarters to somewhere with a better airport and a larger consumer market. The local economy will benefit from the salaries of the engineers and the spending of the VCs, but the equity value will accrue to people who are not residents. The city that builds the incubator is, in a sense, building a farm that feeds a harvest that goes elsewhere. This is not a reason not to build it. But it is a reason to be clear-eyed about what the return on the investment actually is, and to resist the framing that says building the hub will make the city "the next San Francisco." It will make the city a place where some people do important work for a while. That is worth having. It is not the same thing as the myth.

prompt: Last week I wrote about funding structures that line up innovation with business, and the most common reply was 'isn't that what B Corps are for?' Write a follow-up post on why 'doing good' shouldn't be defined by tax status or labels.
response:
You asked, in the comments last week, "isn't that what B Corps are for?" It's the first thing anyone says when I describe a funding structure where the company's next round of capital depends on hitting a public impact metric. Fair question. The B Corp label was designed to do roughly what I was describing: force a company to put social and environmental outcomes on the same page as revenue, and make those outcomes visible to outside parties.

But here's the problem. A B Corp certification is a score. You fill out a balance scorecard covering governance, workers, community, environment, and customers. You get a number. You keep the number above a threshold. You renew. The score is a compliance document. It tells me the company answered a set of questions in 2019 and again in 2024. It does not tell me what the company is doing for the world this year, whether that thing is the right thing, or whether the people making decisions inside the company actually weigh externalities when they're choosing between two product launches.

A 501(c)(3) is the same move in a different costume. The IRS verified that the entity fits a legal category. That's it. The category is "charitable, educational, scientific, or religious." A disease-research lab and a country club can both hold that tax status. The label is a filing. It is not an assessment of whether the work being done is the highest-leverage good available to the people funding it.

You might object, and this is the strongest version of the defense, that without the label I'm back to trusting management's word. "We're doing good" is a claim any CEO can make over coffee. The B Corp score at least requires a third party to look at the books. And you'd be right that it's better than nothing. But "better than nothing" is a low bar, and the label has a cost that's easy to miss: it ends the conversation. "We're a B Corp" is a complete sentence. It closes the topic. The person asking "what are you actually doing for the people this product affects?" has received their answer. They don't get to ask the follow-up, because the follow-up implies the label wasn't enough, and nobody wants to be the one who says that to a company wearing its certification on its website like a medal.

The real question underneath "what good are you doing" is "what is the structure of your incentives, and does it force you to keep doing the good when it's expensive?" A company that ties a specific executive's compensation to a measurable community outcome, that has a board seat whose mandate is to veto decisions that externalize costs onto a defined population, that has a funding structure where the investors in round three can pull capital if a published metric slips—that company has built a machine that produces the behavior even when the founder is tired, even when the market shifts, even when the B Corp renewal team is out sick. The label is a photograph of the machine. The machine is what runs.

I'll be honest about where I'm uncertain: I don't know whether B Corp certification actually changes day-to-day decisions inside certified companies, or whether it's mostly a marketing and recruiting signal that happens to correlate with slightly better ESG scores. There's some research in both directions, and I haven't seen a study I'd bet a decision on. What I do know is that the certification process measures a company's posture toward a checklist. It does not measure whether the company's capital allocation, hiring, and product decisions are being shaped by the same values the checklist describes. Those are different things, and the gap between them is where most of the actual harm lives.

So when I say "doing good" shouldn't be defined by tax status or label, I'm not saying labels are useless. They're useful the way a building code is useful: they set a floor below which you can't legally claim to be a certain kind of entity. But a building code doesn't tell you whether the building is a good one. It tells you the walls won't fall down. The question of whether the building is worth building, whether it's in the right place, whether the people who'll live in it actually needed it—that's a question no certification body is equipped to answer, and no company should get to skip it by pointing at a logo.

The follow-up to "isn't that what B Corps are for?" isn't "no, B Corps are bad." It's "yes, and that's not the same thing as the question I was asking." The label is the floor. The structure is the building. I was describing the building.

prompt: Why do street drugs like ketamine and MDMA keep turning out to be better psychiatric treatments than what pharmaceutical companies produce on purpose? I want a speculative blog post that tries a few explanations and says honestly where they might fail.
response:
# The Pipeline Isn't Broken. It's Answering a Different Question.

The premise of the question is slightly off, and the correction matters. Pharmaceutical companies don't set out to "produce psychiatric treatments" the way a bakery sets out to produce bread. They set out to produce molecules that bind to a target, show a signal in a 6-week randomized trial, have a safety profile that won't get them killed in Phase 3, and can be sold as a once-daily pill to millions of people with a patent that lasts 20 years. That's a specific engineering problem. It happens to overlap with "treat depression" in some cases and not in others.

Ketamine and MDMA look like they beat the pipeline because they were never candidates for it.

**The mechanism problem**

The pipeline screens for a clean pharmacological story. You hit this receptor, this downstream pathway activates, this symptom improves. You can draw the arrow in a slide for the FDA.

Ketamine's antidepressant effect doesn't have that arrow. It's an NMDA receptor antagonist, which is well-established. But the thing that actually seems to relieve depression appears to be a downstream cascade: a burst of glutamate in the prefrontal cortex, a spike in BDNF, the growth of new dendritic spines on pyramidal neurons. This happens over hours. The "mechanism" is a remodeling event, not a receptor occupancy. A drug-discovery screen that measures "does this compound bind to NMDA with an IC50 of X" will tell you ketamine does that. It won't tell you that the useful thing is what the brain does with that binding six hours later, and you can't screen for it in a 96-well plate.

MDMA is worse, in a different way. The therapeutic effect in PTSD isn't "serotonin reuptake inhibition." It's that the drug lowers the emotional reactivity of the amygdala enough, for a few hours, that a person can sit with a traumatic memory and a therapist without the memory hijacking the session. The drug is a tool for a process. The active ingredient is arguably the process, not the molecule. You can't put a process in a pill. You can't run a 28-day trial where the endpoint is "did the patient integrate the memory of being assaulted in 1994."

So the pipeline doesn't produce these drugs because the pipeline's question is "find a molecule with a clean, patentable, scalable mechanism," and the answer to that question for depression is still, basically, the same serotonin reuptake trick from the 1980s with a better side-effect profile. The pipeline is good at its question. The question is wrong for these conditions.

**The street-drug feedback loop**

There's a second, less flattering explanation. The people who find ketamine helpful are not a random sample. They've exhausted the pipeline's offerings. They're in the treatment-resistant tail, the 60-70% for whom the SSRI didn't work, or the MAOIs, or the ECT. They go looking. They find an underground clinic or a peer group. They try the drug. They notice, within hours, whether it did something. The feedback loop is fast, personal, and uncontrolled.

That loop has a cost. There are people who took ketamine for depression and got three days of dissociation, a bad trip, and a new fear of going to sleep. Nobody files that in a registry. There's no one to tell the next person. The visible track record of street drugs is the track record of the people who kept talking about it, which is mostly the people it worked for.

The pipeline, by contrast, reports its failures. We know the SSRI works for maybe a third of the people who take it. We know the other two-thirds got a modest placebo effect or nothing. That honesty makes the pipeline look worse than it is, relative to the curated anecdotes of the street-drug world.

This explanation is real but incomplete. It doesn't explain why the double-blind ketamine trials still show a significant effect over placebo. There's a pharmacological component that's genuine. But the size of the effect in open-label settings, where patients know they're getting the "real" ketamine, is noticeably larger than in double-blind ones. The context is part of the drug. The pipeline is designed to strip context out.

**The business model is the mechanism**

This is the one that's hardest to argue with and easiest to get wrong.

Esketamine, the nasal-spray version of ketamine, was approved in 2019. It works for a subset of people with treatment-resistant depression. The effect lasts a few days to a week. You have to administer it in a clinic, monitor blood pressure for two hours, and watch for dissociation. You can't mail it. You can't build a brand around it the way you can around a pill. The revenue per patient per year is a fraction of what a once-daily SSRI generates, because the treatment is episodic, not chronic.

MDMA-assisted therapy is worse for the business model. The MAPS trials showed large effect sizes for PTSD, in the range of 0.8 to 0.9, which is enormous by psychiatric standards. But the intervention is a two-hour session, a few times, with a trained therapist in the room. The "drug" is a facilitator. You can't patent the molecule (it's known, it's been around since the 1940s). You can't patent the therapy protocol in a way that generates the kind of royalty stream that justifies a billion-dollar R&D outlay. The thing that actually works is a combination of a cheap molecule, a specific therapeutic protocol, and a human being who costs $200 an hour. No pharma board wants to build a company around that.

So the pipeline doesn't produce these treatments because the economic structure of the pipeline is antithetical to them. This is true. But it's also a partial story, because it implies that if the economics were different, the drugs would appear. Maybe. But it also lets the pipeline off the hook for the harder question, which is that the "one molecule, one receptor, one pill" model maps poorly onto the actual structure of psychiatric suffering. Cardiovascular disease is a pipeline-friendly problem. A clogged artery is a clogged artery. You can make a stent, you can make a statin, the mechanism is legible, the patient takes a pill, done. "A person cannot stop replaying the memory of a car crash and their body is in a permanent fight-or-flight state" is not a problem with a receptor. It's a problem with a narrative the brain is stuck running. The pipeline has no category for that.

**Where the whole framing breaks**

The question assumes a binary: street drugs on one side, pharmaceutical company output on the other, and the first side is winning. That binary is false in at least two ways.

Ketamine was a pharmaceutical company product. Parke-Davis developed it in the 1960s as an anesthetic, partly because it was cheaper and more stable than the existing options. The antidepressant use was found outside the company, by clinicians and patients, decades later. The pipeline made the molecule. The pipeline did not make the use. That distinction matters, because it means the pipeline's failure wasn't in chemistry. It was in not following the molecule after it left the building.

And "street drugs" includes a lot of things that are genuinely worse and more dangerous than the prescription alternatives. The person who snorts methamphetamine to stay awake is not in the same category as the person who takes a single dose of ketamine in a monitored clinic for treatment-resistant depression. Lumping them together because they share a legal status obscures the actual point, which is about specific molecules with specific pharmacological properties that the development pipeline is structurally ill-equipped to find and deliver.

I'm speculating on the relative weight of each of these explanations. The honest answer is probably that they're all true and they compound each other. The pipeline's screening methods miss the mechanism. The business model punishes the delivery method. The regulatory structure (scheduling, clinic requirements, inability to advertise) adds friction. And the comparison we make is structurally unfair, because we compare the best street-drug outcomes against the average pipeline outcome. None of this is a conspiracy. No one is sitting in a room deciding not to develop ketamine for depression. The incentives are just pointed at a different target, and the target happens to be the wrong one for the problems that actually need solving.

Let me think about what I actually think here.

First, the premise needs a small correction. It's not that these drugs are "better psychiatric treatments than what pharmaceutical companies produce on purpose." The more accurate framing is: these drugs have specific pharmacological properties that happened to be useful for certain psychiatric conditions, and they were discovered/rediscovered through a different pathway than the standard drug-development pipeline. The pipeline is designed to find drugs that do one thing, are safe, are patentable, and have a clear mechanism. Street drugs are found by accident and used by people who don't care about mechanism.

Let me think about the actual explanations:

1. **The pipeline is optimized for the wrong target.** Pharma develops drugs to hit a specific receptor and show a clean signal in a short trial. Ketamine's antidepressant effect doesn't fit this model. It's an NMDA receptor antagonist, but its antidepressant effect seems to come from a cascade of downstream events (BDNF release, synaptic plasticity) that take hours and aren't the "mechanism" in the way a receptor-binding assay shows it. The pipeline screens for binding affinity and functional readouts. A drug that works by making the brain do something 6 hours later, through a pathway nobody can point to cleanly, gets discarded in Phase 1 or 2. MDMA is similar: its therapeutic effect in PTSD seems to involve making it possible to process traumatic memory in a specific therapeutic context, not "blocking a serotonin reuptake." The drug is a tool for a therapy, not a therapy itself.

2. **The street-drug pathway filters for something the pipeline doesn't care about.** People who use ketamine recreationally or in underground clinics are self-selecting. They're trying it for a reason. The feedback loop is fast and personal. You take it, you notice whether it helped. There's no 28-day double-blind trial. There's also a willingness to tolerate weird side effects and a less-than-perfect experience in exchange for a real effect. The pipeline requires a drug to be "clean" enough that a 52-year-old with comorbid diabetes can take it safely. That constraint eliminates a lot of interesting molecules.

3. **The comparison is unfair / survivorship bias.** We notice ketamine and MDMA because they work for a subset of people with treatment-resistant conditions. We don't notice the thousands of people who tried ketamine for depression and got nothing but dissociation and a bad trip. The pipeline produces SSRIs that work for maybe 30-40% of depressed patients but are safe enough to prescribe broadly. The "failure rate" of street drugs is invisible because there's no one reporting on it systematically.

4. **The regulatory and economic structure punishes exactly the kind of drug that ketamine and MDMA are.** Ketamine is a Schedule III controlled substance. You can't advertise it. You can't build a brand. The business model for a drug that needs to be administered in a clinic, for a few hours, maybe a few times, is terrible compared to a pill you take every day for years. MDMA-assisted therapy requires a two-hour session with a trained therapist. That's not a pharma business model. Pharma wants a pill. A pill is scalable, patentable, and doesn't require a $300/hour therapist in the room.

5. **The "pharmaceutical companies produce on purpose" framing smuggles in an assumption.** The assumption is that if you point a really good R&D machine at "make a drug for depression," it should produce a better drug than what a chemist in a garage in the 1950s stumbled onto. But the R&D machine is pointed at "make a drug that binds to a receptor, shows a signal in a 6-week trial, has a clean safety profile, and can be sold to 10 million people." That's a different question. The machine is good at the question it's asked.

Now, where do these explanations fail?

- The pipeline explanation fails because the pipeline HAS produced genuinely useful drugs. Ketamine itself was a pipeline product (Parke-Davis, 1960s) as an anesthetic. The antidepressant use was found outside the pipeline. But the pipeline also produced, say, the atypical antipsychotics, which were a real improvement over chlorpromazine. So the pipeline isn't broken, it's just not pointed at the right problems.

- The "street drugs are better" framing fails because we're comparing the best 5% of street-drug outcomes against the average of pipeline outcomes. If you compare the best SSRI for the right patient against the worst ketamine experience, the SSRI wins. The real comparison is: for treatment-resistant depression, where the pipeline has largely failed (we still mostly have the same mechanism from the 1980s), a drug with a different mechanism can do something.

- The economic explanation fails because it's partly true but also partly a story we tell to avoid the harder question: maybe the pipeline's incentives are correct for most drug development (you do want a safe, scalable pill for 10 million people) and the real problem is that psychiatry specifically is a field where the "one pill, one receptor" model doesn't map onto the actual problems. The pipeline works fine for cardiovascular disease. It's less well-suited to, say, the experience of being unable to process a traumatic memory.

- I should be honest that I'm speculating. The actual reasons are probably a mixture of all of these, plus some I haven't thought of, plus the fact that "street drugs" as a category includes a lot of stuff that is genuinely worse and more dangerous than prescription alternatives.

Let me also think about concrete cases. Ketamine: esketamine (Spravato) was approved in 2019 for treatment-resistant depression. It works. But it's nasal spray, administered in a clinic, for a few hours, and the effect lasts days to a week. The business model is brutal. You need a clinic, you need to monitor for dissociation and blood pressure, you can't just mail it to someone. Compare to an SSRI: pill, once daily, no monitoring, infinite scalability. The pipeline produces SSRIs because that's what the economics reward.

MDMA: the MAPS/MDMA-assisted therapy trials for PTSD showed large effect sizes (around 0.8-0.9 in some analyses). But the drug's role is as a facilitator of a specific therapeutic process. The "active ingredient" is arguably the combination of the drug and the therapy. You can't patent a combination of a known molecule and a therapy protocol in the way you can patent a new molecule. The business case is structurally different.

Where I'm unsure: I'm not sure how much of the ketamine antidepressant effect is genuinely a new mechanism versus how much is a powerful placebo/nocebo effect modulated by the clinical context. The open-label studies (where patients know they're getting ketamine) showed bigger effects than double-blind ones. That's a real problem for the "the drug is just better" narrative. But even accounting for placebo, the double-blind effects are still substantial, so there's a real pharmacological component.
