prompt: An economist I read argues that psychiatric illnesses like alcoholism, ADHD and schizophrenia are best understood as unusual preferences rather than diseases, since they don't look like the 'budget constraints' that physical illnesses are. You're a practicing psychiatrist. Write a thorough reply explaining where that argument goes wrong.
response:
You've framed the argument in a way that's more elegant than the version I've seen in the literature, and I want to take it seriously rather than reflexively dismiss it. The core move is this: a broken leg is a budget constraint. It removes options from your feasible set. You cannot run. You cannot climb the stairs. The constraint is external to your preferences; you take it as given and optimize within it. A person with alcoholism, ADHD, or schizophrenia, by contrast, is not missing options. They are *choosing* options—drinking, not focusing, responding to voices—that a person without the condition would not choose. The difference is not in the constraint set but in the utility function. They have unusual preferences. The framework, if you'll allow me to be blunt, treats the chooser as intact and the choice as the datum. And I think that is exactly backwards for the conditions you've named.

Let me start with the one where your argument has the most surface force, because if I can't make the case there I can't make it anywhere. ADHD. A nine-year-old in my clinic who cannot sit still, who is out of his seat before the question is finished, who loses his homework, his keys, his patience, and who is not in pain, not hearing anything, not driven by any dramatic compulsion. He just... can't hold his attention on a boring task. Your framework says: he prefers stimulation. He is optimizing. The inattention is a choice among available options.

But here is what is not true of that child: he does not update. You sit him down. You explain that if he finishes the worksheet he can play outside. You raise the stakes. You tell him his mother will be disappointed. You tell him he will fail the class. The inattention persists, at the same intensity, across every level of consequence. That is not what preferences do. Preferences are the mechanism by which an agent tracks consequences. A person who "prefers" to be inattentive in a way that is impervious to the consequences of inattention does not have a preference. They have a broken circuit. The prefrontal loop that would implement "I want to do the worksheet, therefore I direct my attention to the worksheet" is not completing. The child is already moving before the choice would be. He is not choosing motion over stillness; the stillness is not available to him in the way that the second slice of pizza is available to a person who "prefers" to skip dessert.

You will object, and you should, that I have not distinguished this from a workaholic who will not stop working despite health consequences, or a gambler who will not walk away. The workaholic's preference is rigid. Why is the child's inattention a disease and the workaholic's overwork a value judgment I am entitled to find unwise?

Because the workaholic can take a Tuesday off. Not easily. Not without a fight with themselves. But the choice is present; the agent is at the point of decision; the "I" that wants to rest is in the room and can, if the stakes are high enough, win. The nine-year-old is not at a point of decision. The stillness is not a losing option in a contest he is losing. It is not an option. I can judge the workaholic's preference as unwise because it is a preference. I cannot judge the child's inattention as unwise because there is no agent at the point where the judgment would land. The distinction between a rigid preference and a reflex is the distinction between a value question and a medical one, and your framework has no category for the second.

Now schizophrenia, where the preference framing breaks more spectacularly. A woman in her thirties, three months into a first episode. She hears her father's voice, dead eleven years, telling her she is worthless. She cannot choose not to hear it. She tried. She clamped her hands over her ears. She moved to a different room. The voice was inside. The perceptual event is involuntary in exactly the way that a visual hallucination in a person with temporal lobe epilepsy is involuntary. It is not in her feasible set of experiences the way choosing to listen to a sad song is. It is an input she did not select and cannot deselect.

Your framework locates constraints on the output side: what she can buy, what she can do, what is available to her. But the hallucination is a constraint on the input side, on what she perceives, and your framework does not look there because it was built for agents whose inputs are taken as given. The "choices" she makes downstream—stopping work, isolating, responding to the voice as if it were real—are optimization given a perceptual constraint that you have misclassified as a preference. You have looked at the output and said "she chose to hear her dead father," which is like looking at a person with a tumor that secretes cortisol and saying "she chose to feel anxious." The tumor is the constraint. The anxiety is the optimization. You have found the optimization and missed the tumor.

Alcoholism is the hardest case for me, and I will say so, because the person is literally reaching for the bottle, repeatedly, in situations where they say they do not want to drink. The choice is visible. The agent is at the point of decision. Your framework has its strongest empirical footing here.

But the "choice" is not a choice in the sense your framework needs. The person has, over years, altered their own neurochemistry. The dopaminergic reward pathway has been restructured so that the cue-response loop bypasses the deliberative circuits. The prefrontal signal "I have decided not to drink" arrives, but it is overridden by a compulsive drive that is not modulated by the deliberation. The person's "preference" for alcohol is not a stable utility function that happens to be pointed at the wrong thing. It is a pathology of the preference-formation process. You cannot treat the output as a datum and ignore the generator. And if you do—if you say, in effect, "you prefer to drink, so the solution is to prefer otherwise"—you have done something that is not merely unhelpful. You have done the same thing a doctor would do if they told a person with a broken leg, "you seem to prefer immobility; perhaps you would feel differently if you preferred to run." The pain is not a preference. The craving is not a preference. Both are events happening to the person, and the framework that cannot see them as such is not a more neutral description of the situation. It is a description that has excised the patient.

I will be honest about where the boundary is blurry. A person with mild ADHD who functions reasonably well, in a job that suits their need for stimulation, in a relationship that tolerates their forgetfulness—where do you draw the line between a neurodevelopmental difference and a disease? My clinical criterion is impairment, and impairment is a judgment call, and I have made the wrong call. I have medicated a kid who needed a different classroom, and I have failed to medicate a kid who needed a stimulant. The line is not where your framework needs it to be, and I don't think your framework helps me draw it. "Preference" and "impairment" do not track each other. A person can have a severe difference and no impairment because the environment is structured around it. Does that make it not a disease? I am not sure. But I am sure it is not a preference, because the person cannot choose to be different.

The deepest error, I think, is in the unit of analysis. Your framework's unit is the choice. It assumes a chooser, takes the chooser as given, and examines the choices the chooser makes. In psychiatry, the unit is often the *capacity to choose*. The question is not "what did the patient choose?" but "could the patient have chosen otherwise, and what would it have cost them, and where did the process break?" You cannot diagnose a problem with the choice if you have assumed the chooser is intact. That is not a small methodological point. It is the whole difference between a doctor and an actuary.

The "choice" to respond to it—to become withdrawn, paranoid, to stop working—is downstream of a constraint that the preference framework cannot see because it's looking for the constraint in the wrong place. prompt: Someone wrote to a famous songwriter saying she didn't know who she was and so couldn't make art. He told her she didn't need to know. Write an essay on whether self-knowledge matters for creative work, and how people actually come to know themselves.
response:
The advice is good, and it is also a trap, and the person who gave it probably knew that.

You do not need to know who you are before you make the first thing. No one does. The idea that you should sit down, complete some internal audit, arrive at a settled answer about your temperament and your wounds and your values, and only then pick up the pen or the guitar or the chisel—that idea has stopped most people who ever wanted to make something from ever making it. And the reason it stops them is not that the audit is hard. It's that the audit has no bottom. You can keep finding new contradictions, new layers, new "but actually I think what I really mean is." The self is not a document you finish and then submit. It is a process, and the process doesn't pause while you're reading the terms and conditions. So the songwriter is right that you should start. You should start badly, early, before you feel ready, and the not-feeling-ready is not a defect in the plan. It is the plan.

Where the advice goes wrong is in the word "know." It treats knowing yourself as a single event, a threshold you either cross or don't, and by framing it that way it lets you skip past the actual thing that happens, which is slower and less dramatic. You don't find out who you are. You find out a few things, one at a time, mostly by accident, and the finding-out changes what you can do next.

A novelist writes her third book and reads it back and realizes she has written the same argument with her mother in all three books, dressed in different settings. That realization is not a prerequisite to writing. It is a consequence of having written. Before it, she had a story she was telling herself about what she was writing: a story about grief, or about small towns, about whatever the marketing copy would say. After it, she knows something more specific and more uncomfortable: that she is not writing about grief. She is writing about the specific sound of her mother's voice when she is not angry, which is the sound she has been trying to avoid for twenty years. The knowledge didn't come from sitting with a journal. It came from noticing a pattern in her own output, which is a form of attention that is harder and more useful than introspection, because introspection can stay in the realm of plausible generalities while a pattern in your work is a fact. You wrote the same line three times. That's not a metaphor. That's a line.

This is where the objection lands hardest. The best work is often the earliest work, and the earliest work was made by someone who knew very little. Dylan at twenty. The first novels. The early canvases. If self-knowledge is what separates the real work from the competent work, you can't explain why the real work showed up first, before there was any knowledge to draw on.

I think the explanation is that the early work has a different kind of knowledge, and it is real. The twenty-year-old doesn't know who she is in the reflective sense. She hasn't had time to build the self-narrative, to sort the evidence, to decide which of her impulses are "her" and which are just what she's been fed. But she knows what she can't help doing. She knows that the thing she is building is the only thing she can build, in the way that a river knows its course before anyone draws a map. That knowledge is not nothing. It is the knowledge of constraint, and constraint is what makes a thing specific rather than generic. The early work is extraordinary not because the artist is self-aware but because she is not yet compromised. She hasn't learned what's safe. She hasn't internalized the taste of the audience. She is still doing the thing she can't help doing, and the not-helping is a kind of knowledge that no amount of reflection will produce, because reflection is the thing that lets you choose the safe version.

So the relationship is not a sequence. It's not: know yourself, then create. And it's not: create, and the knowing is irrelevant. It's a loop, and the loop takes years to turn. You make a thing. You look at it. You notice what you actually did, as opposed to what you meant to do. The gap between those two is where the knowledge lives. You make the next thing, and the gap is slightly different, and you notice a new thing. Over a decade this adds up to a person who knows, in a working and practical sense, what she is for. Not a fixed identity. A set of constraints and attractions that she can feel in her hands when she's doing the work.

How people actually come to know themselves, then, is mostly through friction with the thing they're making. Not through the thing they're making being good. Through the thing being specific. A vague painting teaches you nothing about yourself. A painting where you agonized for a week over whether the background should be that particular grey teaches you that you are a person who cannot let a color be merely a color, that you need the color to be doing a job, that your tolerance for decoration is lower than you thought. The knowledge is in the doing, in the choosing, in the small decisions that accumulate into a style, and the style is the self, visible.

There is a limit, though, and I think the songwriter's advice, however well-intentioned, can help you miss it. If you make the same thing for thirty years and call it a journey of self-discovery, you are not discovering. You are confirming. The knowledge only comes if you look at your own work with some degree of honesty and notice that you are doing the same thing, and then find a way to do something else. The noticing is the hard part. Not the doing. The doing is easy. Anyone can make the thing they already know how to make. The knowing is in the noticing, and the noticing requires you to be less in love with your own work than you would like to be.

She didn't need to know who she was to write the first song. She will need to know, eventually, to write the one that matters. The first song is permission. The later one is the point.

prompt: Everyone in crypto is proposing new governance models, but they nearly all boil down to some form of voting. Write a post questioning that: what's wrong with voting as a governance mechanism, especially for decentralized communities, and what could replace it?
response:
The Uniswap governance vote on changing the protocol fee is not a governance event. It is a recommendation. The vote goes to a number. The number is displayed on a website. Then a multisig of five addresses either signs a transaction matching that number or it doesn't. If the vote says 0.30% and the multisig signers think 0.30% will spook their LPs, the multisig signs for 0.25% and the vote is a footnote. Nobody audits the multisig. Nobody can. The "governance" is the five keys. The vote is a way of making the five keys feel like they're responding to something.

This is not an anomaly. It's the structural truth of token voting in a protocol where the code doesn't read the ballot. MakerDAO is the exception, because its contracts do read the vote on risk parameters. But even there, the vote is token-weighted, which means the people with the largest exposure to the parameter setting get the largest say. The entity that has $200 million in MKR and is sensitive to a 5% change in the stability fee gets 200 times the voice of the person who staked 20 MKR to get a discount on a loan. The vote is a mechanism for the people most affected by the decision to make the decision. That sounds like a feature. It's also the reason the 2020 near-death-spiral wasn't caught by governance: the large holders' incentives were to keep the system stable enough to protect their positions, not to adjust risk parameters at the speed the market was moving. The fix that actually saved Maker wasn't a vote. It was the liquidation engine and the DSA circuit breakers, which are hard-coded and don't take a poll.

So what is voting actually for in these communities? The standard answer is coordination. Without a vote, every disagreement forks. The chain fragments. Liquidity scatters. Development splits. The network effects that make the protocol valuable in the first place dissolve. Voting is how you keep everyone on one track.

That's true, and it's the strongest case for the mechanism. But notice what it actually does. It keeps everyone on one track by letting a subset of the community make the decision and calling the result the community's will. The subset is whoever shows up to the vote, which is whoever has a large enough position or a strong enough ideological commitment to spend the time. The speculator who bought UNI in March to ride a chart doesn't vote. The person using the protocol as a daily tool doesn't vote. The people who vote are the ones for whom the protocol is a portfolio position or a project. Their preferences are not the preferences of the user base. They are the preferences of the stakeholders. And the stakeholders' preference is, in the abstract, for the protocol to keep existing and keep accruing value. That's a reasonable preference. It's just not a democratic one, and calling it one doesn't make it so.

The deeper problem is that voting is a mechanism for resolving disputes within a polity, and a decentralized protocol is not a polity. A polity is a group of people who have agreed to be bound by a collective decision they didn't personally make. You pay taxes you don't want to pay because you accepted the compact. The user of a decentralized protocol never accepted that compact. They installed a client or connected a wallet. They are interacting with software. The person voting on whether to add a new governance parameter to the protocol has no standing to bind the person who will be using that parameter next Tuesday. There is no social contract. There is a smart contract, and the smart contract's relevant clause is the one that lets you withdraw your funds at any time.

That clause is the actual governance mechanism. The fork is the ballot. If you don't like the parameter, you take your stake, your users, your developers, and you build the other version. Ethereum didn't have a governance vote in July 2016. The DAO was hacked, the community was split, and the resolution was a hard fork executed by the people who controlled the node software. The minority that wanted the chain to remain unmodified got a chain. They still have it. They call it Ethereum Classic. Nobody voted for that. The market for the fork did the voting. It's a brutal mechanism. The Ethereum Classic chain has a small market cap and a small community. The minority lost the market-selection vote. But they lost it with their assets intact, which is the only protection a decentralized system can actually guarantee. No ballot provides that. A vote can tell you that 60% prefer the other outcome. It cannot prevent you from being on the losing side of a chain that's still running code you didn't consent to.

So what replaces the vote? Not a better vote. Quadratic voting, reputation-weighted voting, delegated voting, liquid democracy—these are all votes with different weights. They change the distribution of power among the people who show up. They don't change the fact that the people who show up are the stakeholders, not the users, and that the decision binds people who weren't in the room.

What replaces it is fewer decisions that need to be made collectively. The consensus layer—the rules of the ledger, the settlement finality, the upgrade process—should be as close to hard-coded as possible. Change it on a timescale of years, through a process so difficult that it functions as a constitution rather than a policy debate. Bitcoin's upgrade process is, in practice, a consensus among a handful of core developers and the mining community, reached over months or years through public argument. It's not a vote. It's a slow technical negotiation backed by the implicit threat that if you ship a broken upgrade, the network doesn't adopt it. That threat is the real check. It doesn't require a ballot. You list it, subject to the risk parameters the protocol's code enforces. The "governance" question dissolves into a permissionless-building question. They get a result, and then the protocol moves on, and their preference is not on the books anywhere. On a fork, at least the preference is instantiated in code. The chain exists. It might be small. It might grow. The 10% who wanted the other fee on a fork have a working product that does what they wanted. The 10% who lost the vote have a thread on a forum explaining why 0.30% was better.

The vote is how a community decides. A protocol is not a community. It's a set of rules people choose to live under, one at a time, with their exit always open. The governance that matches that reality isn't a ballot. It's a conflict-resolution device within a shared community. But a decentralized protocol's user base isn't a community in that sense. It's a set of people who happen to interact through the same software. The person using Uniswap to swap ETH for DAI on a Tuesday afternoon has no relationship to the person who's voting on whether to add a new fee parameter. Voting forces a collective decision onto people who never consented to be governed collectively. It's the architecture of the protocol itself—what's hard-coded, what's parameterized, what's forkable. The fork IS the governance mechanism. If you don't like the decision, you take your stake and your users to the fork. That's how it actually works in practice. Ethereum didn't have a governance vote in 2016. People forked. The "veto" in a decentralized system is the fork, not the ballot.

If every disagreement produces a fork, you fragment liquidity, you fragment development, you create a coordination nightmare. But here's where I think the steelman actually undermines itself: the reason voting keeps people on one track isn't democratic legitimacy. It's that the voting process is captured by the people with the most to lose from forking—large holders, foundations, early backers. So "voting prevents fragmentation" is really "voting lets a small group make the decision and call it the will of the community." 1. Make the protocol more forkable. Reduce the switching cost of forking. If forking is cheap, you don't need a vote to resolve every disagreement. The consensus layer (what the rules of the ledger are) should be as hard-coded as possible, changed only through a process so slow and difficult that it's effectively a constitution. The fork that gets the most developers and liquidity wins, and everyone else is stranded on a dead chain. prompt: It's the day before the 2016 US election and the race looks close. I'm worried everyone will draw sweeping conclusions about the country from whichever way it falls. Write a short essay on how we should think about what the result will mean.
response:
The worry is easy to state. Tomorrow, one of two people gets the keys to the government, and by Wednesday the country will be full of people explaining what it *means*. The word "means" is doing enormous unexamined work in that sentence. It treats a number produced by a specific mechanism as though it were a reading of a national pulse, a verdict, a sentence passed. It isn't any of those things. It's a count.

A presidential election is, mechanically, the act of a subset of the population. Not everyone votes. In 2012, roughly 131 million people out of about 222 million eligible cast ballots. Of those, the ones who mattered most were the ones in a dozen or so states where the Electoral College math actually turns. Pennsylvania, Ohio, Florida, Virginia, North Carolina, Iowa, New Hampshire, Colorado, New Mexico, Wisconsin. The rest of the country is context. So when people say "the country voted," the more accurate sentence is "the people who showed up in a handful of swing states, on a Tuesday in November, in the middle of a particular economic situation, with a particular set of issues that had dominated the last three debates, chose one of two specific individuals over the other." That is a fact. It is not a diagnosis.

The structure makes sweeping conclusions even harder to justify than the raw number does. In 2012, Obama took 332 electoral votes to Romney's 206, but his popular-vote margin was 51.3 percent. The "meaning" of that result—the end of the postwar consensus, the triumph of one vision of America over another—was really the meaning of a decade of demographic and economic shifts that the election merely registered at one point in time. The election was the index, not the thing indexed. The same will be true tomorrow, whichever way it falls. The number is a snapshot of a longer process, and mistaking the snapshot for the process is how you end up with "this is the turning point" or "this is the end of the republic" when what you actually have is one data point on a trendline you haven't finished drawing.

You might object that this is a cynical framing, that it drains the word *mandate* of all content, and that if a 51 percent result doesn't mean much, then democracy is a farce. I'll grant the premise that a winner has a mandate. A mandate is an authorization: you are now the person who signs the bills, picks the judges, sets the foreign policy. That is real, and it is not nothing. But a mandate is not a diagnosis of the nation's health, and it is not a verdict on the character of the people who voted the other way. "The country has spoken" is a phrase that smuggles in a unity the 50-to-50 split refutes. When the result is close, the most honest reading is that there is no single national mood to be read. There are two, and they roughly cancel. The winner's margin is the residual, and residuals are where measurement error lives.

The conclusions people will draw will be asymmetrical, and that asymmetry is worth watching. The winning side will say the result confirms a trend, corrects a drift, marks a turning point. The losing side will say it is an aberration, a seizure, a warning that the system is broken. Both are projecting a narrative onto a data point. Both are writing the next four years' story in advance, before a single policy has been tested. The data point is: in November 2016, in these conditions, with these two candidates, more people in the decisive states chose X than Y. Everything beyond that sentence is interpretation, and interpretation is where you are allowed to disagree.

So the useful frame for tomorrow morning is not "what does this mean?" but "what does this authorize?" It authorizes one person to try, for four years, to do what they campaigned on, with a legislature that may or may not cooperate, in an economy that will not sit still. It authorizes the other side to watch, criticize, organize, and prepare for the next election. The meaning of the result will be written by what happens after the number, not by the number itself. The number is the starting gun. The race hasn't begun.

prompt: Americans spend more on almonds than on all of election campaigns, which has always puzzled me. Write a post that explains how political money really works, who has figured out how to use it, and what that means for AI regulation.
response:
The almond math doesn't quite work. Americans spend roughly $5 to $6 billion a year on almonds as a consumer good. Total US election spending across federal, state, and local races in a presidential cycle lands closer to $14 or $15 billion. In an off year it drops to maybe $8 to $10 billion. So the "more than all elections" framing is off by a factor of two or three. But the instinct behind the comparison is right, and it points at something worth untangling: why does a nut get to spend like a political movement, and what does that tell us about the people who will shape AI law?

The thing most people get wrong about political money is that they picture a transaction. A check goes in, a vote comes out. A lobbyist buys a senator's dinner and the senator votes for the pesticide exemption. That model is so wrong it's almost useless. What political money actually buys is three things, in roughly this order of importance: access, information, and the management of political risk.

Access means you get into the room before the bill is written. The real work on any regulation happens in the drafting stage, in committee markups, in the phone calls between a staffer and a company's policy director. By the time a bill hits the floor, the compromises are already baked in. The people in the room during drafting get to shape the language, and language is where regulation lives or dies. A 12-word definition of "covered entity" can determine whether your product is regulated or not.

Information is the underrated one. A well-run lobbying shop doesn't just tell a senator what its client wants. It tells the senator what will happen to the senator's district if the regulation passes. It brings the plant manager. It brings the supplier. It builds the narrative that makes a vote feel like a choice between the senator's voters and an abstract future. This is why a $2 million coordinated effort by an industry with 80,000 workers in a single congressional district will outperform a $50 million Super PAC ad buy in the same district. The ad tells voters what to think. The plant manager tells the senator what will happen if she votes wrong.

Political risk management is the strategic layer. The goal is not to pass your preferred bill. The goal is to make it politically dangerous for a legislator to vote for the alternative. You do this by identifying which constituents will bear the cost, making sure they are visible, and making sure the legislator knows that the cost will be attributed to the vote, not to the industry. The almond industry is good at this. Water policy in California is not an abstract environmental question. It is a question about whether the farmer in the Central Valley, who has been there three generations, gets to keep growing. You can run a Super PAC ad about sustainable aquifer management. You cannot run one about the Garcia family losing their orchard.

Who has figured this out? The pattern is consistent across decades. It is industries with concentrated, geographically identifiable stakeholders facing a specific, identifiable regulatory threat. Agriculture. Pharma. Defense contractors. The electric utilities. The oil and gas sector in the states where it is the employer of last resort. These groups have spent forty or fifty years building the infrastructure: the trade associations, the political action committees, the think tanks that produce the "independent" research, the revolving-door pipeline between agency and company. They know which staffers to call, which committee to target, which amendment to support in exchange for which concession. They have a playbook, and the playbook works.

The financial sector is the most instructive modern case. Before 2008, banking regulation was a low-stakes game. After the crisis, the sector understood that the single highest-return investment it could make was in shaping the next regulatory cycle. It poured money into the drafting of Dodd-Frank, into the post-implementation rulemaking, into the state-level preemption fights. The result was a regulatory architecture that was, by the banks' own account, manageable. Not the deregulation they wanted in 2001, but a system they could operate inside. That is what success looks like. You do not get the law you wanted. You get a law you can live with, and the competitors who do not have your lobbying infrastructure get a law they cannot.

Now: what does this mean for AI regulation?

The first thing to notice is that the AI companies themselves are in a weaker political position than their market valuations suggest. OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, Microsoft. Their employees are brilliant, well-paid, and politically engaged, but they are spread across a handful of metro areas and they do not constitute a voting bloc in the way that Central Valley growers constitute one in the 19th District. More importantly, the AI labs do not face a single, clear regulatory threat the way a pharma company faces a drug pricing bill. AI regulation cuts across data privacy, labor, antitrust, national security, export controls, environmental law (data center power consumption), and consumer protection. You cannot build a unified lobbying position when your product touches seven different regulatory domains and seven different agencies.

The groups that will actually shape AI regulation are not the AI labs. They are the infrastructure companies. The electric utilities that are being asked to build out grid capacity for data centers and who will lobby against any regulation that slows deployment, because slowed deployment means their capital projects get delayed. The data center real estate operators. The chip manufacturers, particularly Nvidia and TSMC, who have a concentrated interest in export policy and who already have the lobbying machinery to protect it. The cloud providers. These are companies with existing political infrastructure, with concentrated economic stakes in specific states and districts, and with a clear message: regulation that slows AI deployment slows our returns, which means fewer jobs in our districts.

That message will be effective. It will not be because it is true in every case. It will be because it is legible to a senator whose district has a data center campus and a utility expansion project. The AI safety case, by contrast, is probabilistic and long-horizon. "If we do not regulate this now, something bad might happen in five to fifteen years" is a terrible political argument. It loses to "the data center in your district is going to need 200 megawatts and the utility says the current rules make that impossible."

The hardest objection to this account is the one that says I am underestimating the power of concentrated wealth. The AI labs are worth hundreds of billions of dollars. They can outspend the utilities. They can fund their own think tanks, their own ad campaigns, their own candidate support. And they will, eventually. But money without political architecture is just money. The pharmaceutical industry has more revenue than the AI industry and it took the pharmaceutical industry thirty years of consistent, targeted spending to build the regulatory capture it now enjoys. The AI companies are in year three. They will spend more. They will hire better lobbyists. They will get more access. But the access will be to the same rooms, and the rooms will be shaped by the same dynamics, and the infrastructure companies will already be in them.

What this means in practice is that AI regulation will probably look less like a single federal AI law and more like a patchwork of sector-specific rules shaped by the interests of the companies that are already embedded in the political system. Export controls on chips, because the chip industry is organized. Data center siting rules, because the utilities and local governments are organized. Labor rules around automation, because the unions are organized. And a federal AI framework that is broad in language and narrow in enforcement, because the AI companies will have enough access to prevent anything specific, and the other industries will have enough leverage to prevent anything that threatens their deployment timelines.

The almond growers know something the AI executives are still learning. The regulation you get is not the regulation you argue for in a white paper. It is the regulation that the most politically organized group in the room can live with, and that the least organized group cannot stop. Right now, in the AI policy room, the least organized group is the one with the safety models.
